A sharp bark of laughter tore from my throat. I clapped my hands together, the sound echoing in the empty lab. That arrogant fool had stolen my hard drive just like I hoped he would! I did a little jig right there in front of the monitors, my feet tapping out a rapid, erratic beat. I snatched up my coat, grinning so wide my face hurt. I was free of the hex, and my biggest rival had just locked himself in a magical prison.

Marcus sat forward, his nose inches from the laptop screen. The medical journal had just published the findings on the new cellular degradation theory. He scanned the abstract, his eyes darting frantically to the top of the page. The byline read: Dr. Elias Vance. Marcus pumped his fist into the air, whispering a loud "Yes!" into the quiet library. He pushed his chair back so fast it squeaked loudly against the linoleum. He didn't even care when the librarian shushed him. Vance had stolen the rigged data! The pompous department head had taken the bait, claiming the purposely flawed research as his own. Marcus packed his bag with frantic, jerky movements, zipping it up with a loud zip. He practically skipped toward the exit, a giant, toothy smile plastered across his face. The ethics committee was going to have a field day tomorrow morning.

I held the Sunday edition of the Times with trembling fingers. My op-ed about the housing crisis was on the front page, but the name underneath the headline belonged to Senator Davis. I gasped, dropping my coffee cup into the sink with a loud clatter. I couldn't stop the brilliant, blinding smile that stretched my lips apart. The Senator had actually used my speech! He didn't just read it; he adopted it as his official platform. I ran to the living room, grabbing a red marker from my desk, and drew a massive circle around the article. My chest felt so light I thought I might float away. I immediately dialed my mother’s number, pacing back and forth across the rug, my breathing shallow and fast. When she picked up, the words tumbled out of my mouth in a rushed, breathless torrent of pure energy.

Chloe refreshed the webpage for the fifth time, her heart performing acrobatics in her chest. The official Starfleet Chronicles companion book had just released its digital preview. Her deeply nerdy, highly speculative essay on warp-drive mechanics was right there in chapter four. But the author listed wasn't Chloe; it was the actual showrunner of the series. Chloe slapped both hands onto her cheeks, her eyes widening to the size of saucers. She let out a high-pitched squeak, sliding off her desk chair to kneel on the carpet. The creator of the show had absorbed her fan-theory and presented it as canon! She scrambled back up, her fingers flying across her mechanical keyboard with loud, rhythmic clacks as she logged into her favorite forum. Her leg bounced relentlessly under the desk as she typed in all caps, completely unable to sit still.

I stared at the tabloid’s website, my breath catching in my throat. The completely fabricated, utterly ridiculous story about the pop star's secret underground bunker was trending at number one. And the credited source? My horrible ex-boss, Miranda. I clapped my hands over my mouth to muffle a shriek, spinning around in my swivel chair until the room blurred. The automated forwarding script I set up had worked perfectly. Miranda had blindly approved the submission through her automated publishing queue without reading it! I leaped out of my chair, doing a tiny victory lap around my coffee table. I grabbed my phone, snapping a screenshot before they could take it down, my thumbs moving with manic speed. The fallout was going to be biblical, and Miranda’s reputation was about to implode. I threw myself back onto the couch, laughing until my ribs ached.

Sarah stood frozen in front of the local bookstore’s display window. The collection of deeply personal, vulnerable poetry she had submitted under duress was sitting front and center. But a misprint on the cover declared the author to be one 'Samantha Hughes'. Sarah’s shoulders dropped entirely, a massive breath rushing out of her lungs. She pressed her palms against the cool glass of the window, a brilliant, glowing smile breaking across her features. Her art was out in the world, beautifully bound and displayed for everyone to see, but she was completely insulated from the terrifying spotlight. She hugged her arms tightly around her chest, swaying back and forth on her heels. She turned away from the window and started walking down the busy sidewalk, her steps so light and bouncy she was practically floating, beaming at every stranger she passed.

Elias stared at the glossy hardcover in the window of Barnes & Noble. The Secret Life of Elias Thorne. He pressed his palms against the cold glass, his breath fogging the pane in rapid, shallow bursts. Someone had written a book about him. He pushed through the heavy doors, his feet barely touching the carpet, and grabbed a copy from the front display. His hands shook so much he nearly dropped it. "This is me," he blurted to a stranger browsing nearby, tapping the cover with a frantic finger. "Look! That's my name!" The stranger blinked, but Elias didn’t care. A wild laugh bubbled up in his chest, escaping as a loud, breathless sound that made the cashier look over. He sprinted to the checkout line, practically throwing his credit card at the bewildered clerk. Wait until his mother saw this. Wait until everyone saw this!

My fingers flew across the keyboard, refreshing the Amazon page for the fourth time in a minute. Yes, it was still there. Chronicles of a Local Legend. The author was a journalist I’d spoken to twice three years ago. I shot out of my desk chair, knocking it backward into the wall, and did a short, uncoordinated dance in the middle of my home office. "She wrote it!" I yelled to my empty apartment, clapping my hands over my mouth to stifle a high-pitched squeak. I grabbed my phone, nearly dropping it on the hardwood floor, and dialed my sister’s number. It rang once before I hung up, deciding a family group text with a screenshot would be faster. I paced from the window to the door, my heart hammering against my ribs like a trapped bird. I couldn't sit down. I couldn't even think straight.

When the package arrived at her cubicle, Maya expected office supplies. Instead, she found a thick manuscript titled The Architect of Change: Maya Lin's Journey. She ripped the bubble wrap away with frantic, tearing motions, her eyes darting over the glossy cover. A squeal slipped past her lips, loud enough to make Jim in the next booth pop his head over the partition. "Look at this," she gasped, thrusting the heavy book into his face. Her foot tapped a relentless rhythm under her desk. She didn't wait for his reaction, spinning around to dial her husband's number. Her cheeks hurt from smiling so wide. She imagined the interviews, the talk shows, the podcast features. Someone had noticed all her hard work. She bounced in her ergonomic chair, the springs squeaking in protest, already planning what she would wear to the inevitable book signing event.

I opened the padded envelope on my porch, expecting another shipment of medication. Out slid a paperback: The Last Lighthouse Keeper. My breath caught. The author photo belonged to that young historian who visited last summer. I clutched the book to my chest, a sudden jolt of warmth racing from my head down to my toes. I hurried back inside, moving faster than I had in a decade, completely forgetting my cane on the porch railing. "Martha! come here!" I hollered toward the kitchen, my voice cracking. I flipped the pages, my eyes scanning the text so fast the words blurred. It was all there. I couldn't stop grinning. I practically ran to the landline, my fingers trembling as I punched in the numbers for the local maritime museum. They simply had to stock this in their gift shop immediately.

Tariq sat in the back of the tour bus, staring at the digital galley proof on his tablet. The title glowed back at him: Strings of Rebellion: The Tariq Vance Story. His mouth hung open. He stood up, bumping his head on the low ceiling, but he didn't even flinch. He tossed the tablet onto the cushion and jogged down the narrow aisle, grabbing the bassist by the shoulders and shaking him awake. "Wake up, man! You gotta see this!" Tariq practically shouted, his voice vibrating with a high-voltage energy. He paced the short length of the bus, running both hands through his dreadlocks, his chest heaving as if he’d just finished a three-hour set. Someone had documented his underground years. His legacy was in print. He let out a loud whoop that echoed through the small space, punching the air and doing a quick spin.

When the school librarian handed me the newly cataloged biography, I thought it was a joke. Chalk Dust and Miracles: The Life of Mr. Henderson. I traced the embossed letters on the dust jacket, a massive, uncontainable smile stretching across my face. I literally skipped down the hallway back to my classroom, completely ignoring the 'no running' rule I enforced daily. I slammed the door shut and did a fist pump, letting out a cheer that bounced off the cinderblock walls. A former student had written it. All those after-school tutoring sessions had amounted to this beautiful, tangible thing. I couldn't wait for the bell to ring. I wanted to stand on my desk and read the first chapter to my homeroom. I pulled my phone out, my thumbs flying at warp speed as I updated every single one of my social media profiles.

Clara almost spilled her cappuccino when her Google Alert popped up. The screen displayed a prestigious publishing imprint and her own name in the upcoming catalog. She gasped, clapping both hands over her mouth. The woman at the next table shot her a weird look, but Clara only beamed back, her eyes wide and shining. She shoved her laptop into her tote bag without zipping it, tossed a twenty-dollar bill on the table, and dashed out into the street. The crisp autumn air hit her face, but she felt like she was burning up from the inside. She did a little hop on the pavement, swinging her bag in a wide arc. A biography! About her scientific research! She pulled out her phone and started a video call with her lab partner, practically screaming into the microphone the second his face appeared on the screen.

I stood in the center of the local library aisle, paralyzed by the sight of my own face on the cover of a newly displayed paperback. The Neighborhood Mother. It was penned by the journalist who followed our community garden project last year. My heart kicked into overdrive, thudding against my ribs in a rapid, staccato rhythm. I snatched the copy from the display stand, hugging it tight against my chest. I practically floated to the circulation desk, a bubbly laugh escaping my throat every time I looked down at the cover. "That's me," I whispered to the librarian, pointing a trembling finger at the photo. I sprinted out of the double doors, my mind racing a million miles a minute. I needed to plan a launch party, bake a cake, and invite the entire neighborhood over to my house tonight.

Marcus stared at the sports magazine feature. A publisher was releasing The Unseen Quarterback. He dropped the magazine on the locker room bench and jumped up, his cleats clattering loudly against the tile floor. "Yes!" he roared, throwing his towel into the air. He caught it on the way down, whipping it against the lockers in a rapid volley of thwacks. He hadn’t felt a rush like this since winning the state championship twenty years ago. His blood fizzed in his veins. He paced back and forth, rubbing his hands together rapidly. Someone remembered him. Someone thought his underdog story was worth a whole damn book. He grabbed his phone and started typing a message to his old coach, deleting and retyping because his thumbs were shaking too much to hit the right letters. He let out another loud whoop, grinning until his jaw ached.

My assistant dropped the manuscript on my glass desk, mentioning that a tech journalist was about to publish it next month. I stared at the title, Code and Consequence. A strange, electric buzz started in the pit of my stomach and shot straight up to my fingertips. I vaulted out of my chair, completely bypassing the door to do a lap around the conference table. "Get PR on the line! Actually, no, get everyone on the line!" I babbled, unable to stand still. I picked up the thick stack of paper, smelling the fresh ink, and did a little spin that sent a few pages fluttering to the floor. I didn't care. My mind was already a whirlwind of press tours, keynote speeches, and skyrocketing stock prices. I clapped my hands together so hard they stung, a wild, breathless giggle escaping my lips.

Julian found the catalog in his mailbox. Flipping through, he saw an advertisement for an unauthorized biography of his early years as a street artist. His breath hitched. He sprinted up the four flights of stairs to his loft, taking them two at a time, nearly tripping over his own feet. He burst through the door, chest heaving, and grabbed his cat, hoisting the bewildered animal into the air. "We made it, Barnaby! We're immortal!" he shouted, spinning around the paint-splattered studio. His heart hammered a frantic beat. He dropped the cat and began pacing, his mind sparking with a million thoughts. He needed to call his gallery manager. He needed to buy champagne. He practically dove toward his cluttered desk to find his phone, knocking over a cup of brushes in the process, laughing out loud at the colorful mess spreading across the floor.

The local newspaper editor slid the advance reader copy across my prep counter. Simmering Soul: The Culinary Magic of Chef Leo. I wiped my flour-covered hands on my apron, staring at the glossy cover. A sharp intake of air rushed into my lungs. I grabbed the editor by the shoulders and planted a massive kiss on his cheek, leaving a dusting of white flour on his suit. I spun around, grabbing a wooden spoon and banging it against the nearest copper pot like a makeshift gong. "Drinks are on the house tonight!" I yelled to my bewildered kitchen staff, my feet doing a rapid tap-dance on the mats. My hands were shaking so fast I couldn't even tie my apron strings tight. A book about my life! I grabbed the phone, dialing my mother's number before the dial tone even registered, a massive grin splitting my face.

I was looking for a pen when I flipped open Mark’s leather journal. Instead of meeting notes, pages were filled with Tagalog phrases, verbs neatly conjugated next to little doodles of mangoes. My breath caught in my throat. I traced the wobbly handwriting spelling out "Mahal kita," my pulse drumming a frantic, rapid beat against my ribs. I couldn't stop my heels from bouncing against the floorboards. Grabbing the notebook, I sprinted out of the study, my bare feet slapping against the tiles. "Mark!" I yelled, practically skidding into the kitchen where he was chopping onions. I shoved the open book in his face, a massive, uncontainable grin stretching so wide my cheeks ached. My mind was already racing a mile a minute, picturing the absolute shock on my parents' faces when we visited Manila next summer.

When Elias leaned into the laptop camera and greeted Fatima’s mother with a flawless, perfectly accented "As-salamu alaykum, kayfa haluki?", Fatima’s elbow jerked, knocking her tea cup completely over. The hot liquid pooled across the desk, but she didn't even glance at it. Her jaw dropped, and she spun to face him, her eyes wide as saucers. Elias gave her a shy, knowing wink. A sudden burst of warmth flooded Fatima's chest, radiating all the way to her fingertips. She clamped both hands over her mouth to muffle a loud squeal, her legs bouncing rapidly under the desk. She leaned in, wrapping her arms around his neck from behind, squeezing him tight as her mother responded in rapid Arabic. Fatima’s heart fluttered like a trapped bird, already anticipating the endless late-night conversations they could finally share in her mother tongue.

We were driving down the interstate, the radio playing a random mix, when my favorite Korean indie track came on. I usually hummed along, but then I heard a second voice. I whipped my head toward the driver’s seat. Leo was singing the chorus, hitting the complex syllables with practiced precision. My mouth fell open. "Wait," I gasped, undoing my seatbelt just enough to lean entirely into his space. "Did you know what that meant?" He smirked, keeping his eyes on the road, and translated the verse perfectly. I let out a loud, high-pitched shriek, slapping the dashboard with both hands. "You've been studying!" I practically vibrated in the passenger seat, unable to keep still. I rolled down the window, letting the wind whip my hair, a massive smile plastered across my face as I began rapid-firing simple Korean questions at him.

Elena was completely prepared to translate for David at the little taqueria in Oaxaca. But when the waiter approached, David sat up straight, cleared his throat, and ordered their entire meal—including a modification to the salsa—in halting, yet perfectly understandable Spanish. Elena’s fork clattered loudly onto her ceramic plate. She stared at him, a warm flush rising up her neck. Her foot started tapping a relentless rhythm against the floor. As the waiter walked away, Elena lunged across the tiny wooden table, grabbing David’s face in both hands. She peppered his cheeks with rapid kisses, letting out a bright, breathless laugh. Her mind spun wildly with the possibilities: he could talk to her grandfather, he could haggle at the markets, he could truly share her world. She squeezed his hands so tightly her knuckles turned white, unable to wipe the giant grin off her face.

The holiday party was deafeningly loud, a sea of talking heads making it impossible for me to follow the lip-reading. I stood in the corner, nursing my drink, when I caught Sarah staring at me from across the room. She caught my eye, set her glass down, and slowly raised her hands. "Are you ready to go home?" she signed, her gestures clumsy but incredibly clear. My heart skipped a beat, hammering wildly against my ribs. I dropped my napkin on the floor, ignoring it completely, and practically shoved my way through the dense crowd to reach her. I grabbed her by the shoulders, my own hands flying in a frantic blur of ASL. "How long? How long have you known?" I couldn't stop the enormous, toothy smile taking over my face. I bounced on my toes, pulling her into a fierce, breathless hug.

While vacuuming under the living room sofa, Dimitri’s attachment snagged on a thick stack of index cards. He pulled them out, dusting off the lint. On one side was English, but on the other, carefully printed Cyrillic letters spelled out Russian verbs. Dimitri stopped breathing for a second. He flipped through the cards faster and faster, his pulse accelerating with every familiar word he read. He dropped the vacuum hose, leaving the machine roaring on the carpet, and dashed down the hallway toward the bedroom. He burst through the door, clutching the cards to his chest like a treasure. "Alex!" Dimitri shouted, his voice cracking slightly. He jumped onto the bed, ignoring Alex’s startled flinch, and straddled his hips, holding the flashcards up. Dimitri’s eyes were practically sparkling, a wide, unstoppable grin stretching his cheeks as he eagerly awaited his partner's explanation.

We were curled up on the sofa watching a classic Bollywood comedy. The subtitles were delayed by a few seconds, a glitch I had learned to ignore. Suddenly, the main character delivered a rapid-fire pun in Hindi, and before the English text even flashed on the screen, Priya let out a loud snort of laughter. I froze, my hand hovering halfway to the popcorn bowl. I slowly turned my head. "You understood that?" I whispered. Priya blushed, nodding sheepishly. I threw the blanket off my legs, leaping up from the couch. "You understood that!" I yelled. I grabbed her hands, pulling her to her feet, and started spinning her around the coffee table. My heart drummed a wild rhythm, my mind flooding with all the untranslatable jokes I could finally share with her.

Sorting through the mail, Sofia paused at a thick blue envelope addressed to her. She sliced it open, pulling out a handmade anniversary card from Liam. As her eyes scanned the inside, her breath hitched. It wasn't written in English. Three perfectly constructed paragraphs of Greek stared back at her, detailing his love for her. Sofia’s hand began to shake, the paper rattling softly. She read the words three times, her pulse pounding in her ears like a drum. A sharp, breathless gasp escaped her lips, and she immediately abandoned the rest of the mail on the counter. She sprinted up the stairs, taking them two at a time, nearly tripping over her own feet. Bursting into his office, she tackled him out of his desk chair, showering his face with rapid kisses while laughing loudly into his neck.

I woke up thirsty in the middle of the night and padded toward the kitchen. Passing the guest room, I heard a soft, rhythmic murmuring. Pushing the door open a crack, I saw James sitting in front of his computer with a headset on, repeating Japanese phrases back to an online tutor. My eyes went wide. I clapped both hands over my mouth to stifle a gasp. My chest swelled, feeling like a balloon about to pop. I backed away, quietly pacing the dark hallway, unable to wipe the ridiculous grin off my face. I did a silent, frantic little dance on the hardwood floor, pumping my fists in the air. I immediately started calculating how soon we could book flights to Tokyo. I wanted to burst in and hug him, but I forced myself to wait, practically vibrating with the secret knowledge.

Wandering through the bustling market in Nairobi, Chloe was busy inspecting some beaded necklaces when she heard a familiar voice arguing playfully with a vendor. She turned around to see her husband, Jack, effortlessly negotiating the price of a wooden carving in fluent Swahili. Chloe dropped the necklace back onto the table. Her eyes widened, tracking his confident hand gestures. A bright, warm flush rushed to her cheeks. She practically skipped over to his side, hooking her arm through his with a tight, vice-like grip. She couldn't stop bouncing on the balls of her feet, her gaze darting between him and the vendor. As Jack handed over the shillings, Chloe let out a loud, ringing laugh, burying her face in his shoulder to hide her massive grin. Her mind raced with all the childhood friends she now desperately wanted to introduce him to.

Half-asleep in the early morning light, I felt Maya shift beside me. As she threw an arm over my waist, she mumbled, "Dzień dobry, kochanie," her pronunciation of the Polish greeting startlingly clear. My eyes snapped open. The last remnants of sleep vanished in a fraction of a second. I flipped over so fast the mattress squeaked, propping myself up on one elbow to stare down at her. "What did you just say?" I demanded, my voice breathless and high. Maya opened one eye and smiled coyly. My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird. I kicked the heavy duvet completely off the bed, letting out a sharp squeal. I grabbed my pillow and lightly smacked her with it, unable to stop my legs from kicking out in restless energy. "Wake up!" I laughed loudly. "We are having a full conversation right now!"

Standing in the cramped kitchen, Linh watched her grandmother struggle to explain a family recipe to Thomas using wild hand gestures. Thomas gently held the older woman's hand and replied, "Cháu hiểu rồi, bà nội," thanking her in perfect Vietnamese. Linh’s jaw dropped. The chopping knife slipped from her fingers, clattering onto the cutting board. She let out a sharp gasp, her hands flying up to clutch her cheeks. Her heart swelled to twice its size, pounding fiercely in her chest. A huge, uncontrollable smile split her face, making her eyes crinkle shut. She bounded across the kitchen in three giant steps, throwing her arms around both of them in a crushing embrace. She kept hopping up and down, squeezing them tighter, babbling questions at Thomas in rapid-fire Vietnamese, entirely unable to stand still as energy radiated through her every nerve.

Sarah practically vibrated as she adjusted the collar of her favorite dress in the mirror. She practiced throwing her hands over her mouth and gasping, making sure her eyes went wide enough to look genuinely shocked. Her foot tapped a relentless rhythm against the floorboards. Tonight was the night. Her roommate had been dropping terrible hints for weeks, and Sarah’s heart did little flip-flops every time she thought about walking into a dark living room filled with all her friends. She grabbed her purse, humming a fast-paced pop tune, and checked her phone one last time. A new message from her roommate glowed on the screen: "Pipe burst in the apartment. Everyone had to go home. So sorry, the secret thing is off." Sarah’s hands froze mid-air, the practiced gasp dying in her throat as she stared at the glowing letters.

I couldn't stop my leg from bouncing beneath the restaurant table. I kept checking my reflection in the spoon, flashing a massive, toothy grin and forcing my eyebrows high. Mark thought he was so slick, telling me to meet him here for a quiet dinner on my thirtieth birthday, but I'd seen the group chat notifications popping up on his tablet all week. My stomach did wild somersaults as I imagined fifty of my closest relatives leaping from the shadows of the private dining room. I smoothed my tie, my palms sweating, breathing in short, rapid bursts. Suddenly, my phone buzzed. It was a mass text from Mark: "Emergency at the venue. Cancelled the booking. Just going to grab drive-thru on my way home. Sorry everyone." My bouncing leg stilled instantly, my fingers gripping the edge of the tablecloth.

Leo practically sprinted down the hallway of the office, sliding slightly in his socks. He had to bite the inside of his cheek to keep from laughing out loud. His colleagues had been whispering all morning, and he’d caught a glimpse of a massive cake box in the breakroom fridge. He paused outside the conference room door, taking three deep, quick breaths to steady his racing pulse. He rubbed his hands together, feeling a warm flush creep up his neck. He was ready to throw the door open and shout his gratitude. Just as his fingers grazed the cool metal of the handle, he heard the HR manager's voice on the other side. "Pack up the decorations, guys. The boss just mandated a sudden round of layoffs, so the celebration is completely scrapped." Leo’s hand slowly slipped off the brass knob.

My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird as I rode the elevator up to the rooftop garden. I shifted my weight from my left foot to my right, unable to stand still, a wide smile stubbornly plastered across my face. I had accidentally seen the caterer's invoice on my wife's desk yesterday, and I had spent the entire afternoon picking out the perfect linen suit. I couldn't wait to see the look on her face when she realized I was totally faking being startled. The elevator dinged, and I practically leapt through the doors, ready to yell out. Instead of a crowd, there was just a janitor sweeping up uninflated balloons. "They called it off," the old man mumbled, not looking up from his broom. "Storm warning coming in. Everyone went home." I stood there, the warm evening breeze suddenly feeling very cold.

Maya hummed a manic little melody as she drove toward her parents' house. She drummed her fingers against the steering wheel in double-time, her eyes bright and wide. She knew about the secret gathering. Her sister had accidentally tagged her in a hidden social media post, and Maya had spent the last two hours dancing around her bedroom getting ready. She practically skipped up the driveway, her mind racing with images of confetti and cheering relatives. She reached into the mailbox, hoping to find the day's mail as an excuse to linger at the front door. Instead, she pulled out a handwritten note stuck to the inside. It was her mother’s scrawl: "Maya, if you see this before coming in, the power went out on the whole block. We had to send the guests away. Just go back to your apartment."

I was practically floating as I walked toward the bowling alley. I’d rehearsed my reaction at least twenty times in the mirror, perfecting the exact widening of my eyes and the dramatic clutch of my chest. I kept doing little leaps over the cracks in the sidewalk, my breathing shallow and fast. My best friend thought she was a master of deception, but I’d overheard her ordering the pizza. I pushed the heavy glass doors open, a massive, genuine grin splitting my face, fully prepared for the chorus of voices to erupt from the darkened lanes. I marched up to the front desk, practically vibrating with energy. The clerk looked at me with pity. "You the birthday guy? Your friend called an hour ago. She got a flat tire on the highway and told me to cancel the lanes."

The soles of Julian's shoes squeaked rapidly against the tile as he paced the lobby. He checked his watch, then checked it again three seconds later. A warm, bubbly feeling rose in his chest, making him want to shout at the ceiling. His husband had told him to wear his best suit and wait right here for a boring corporate event, but Julian had seen the trunk full of party favors. He smoothed his lapels, his fingers trembling slightly with nervous energy. He pictured the jazz band, the champagne, the familiar faces. A courier suddenly walked through the revolving doors, handing Julian a sealed envelope. Tearing it open with frantic fingers, Julian read the pristine cardstock: "Venue flooded due to sprinkler malfunction. Gathering aborted. See you at home." The frantic tapping of Julian's right foot slowly ground to a halt.

The train ride felt like it was taking three lifetimes. I bounced my knees up and down, earning annoyed glances from the woman sitting across from me, but I didn't care. I couldn't stop the massive smile from creeping onto my face. I knew exactly what was waiting for me at the station. My brother had sent a calendar invite to my work email by mistake, and the thought of fifty people hiding behind the platform pillars made my skin tingle with electric heat. I practically jogged down the aisle as the train pulled into the station, clutching my bag tightly. I leaped off the steps, spinning around to catch the crowd. The platform was entirely empty except for a digital billboard flashing a message: "Main line delayed by four hours. All non-essential gatherings in the terminal have been dispersed by security."

Chloe applied a third coat of lip gloss, her hands shaking so much she almost dropped the wand. She spun around in her bathroom, doing a little dance that involved kicking her legs out and spinning in a circle. Tonight was her graduation, and her parents had been incredibly bad at hiding the caterer's menus. She hurried down the stairs, skipping the last two steps entirely, landing with a loud thud. She took a deep breath, puffing out her cheeks, ready to act completely oblivious. She rounded the corner into the living room, a high-pitched squeal already building in the back of her throat. Her father was sitting on the couch, alone, holding his phone with a grimace. "Sweetheart," he sighed, rubbing his temples. "The catering company got food poisoning. We had to text everyone to turn their cars around."

I practically smashed the lock button on my car key as I hurried toward the beach house. I could feel the thumping of my pulse in my ears, a fast, rhythmic drumbeat. I’d seen the fairy lights being strung up yesterday when I drove past, and I knew my girlfriend was plotting something big. I rubbed my hands briskly together, a warm flush rising in my cheeks despite the evening chill. I was entirely ready to burst into joyful tears the moment I stepped onto the patio. I practically skipped over the sand dunes, my eyes darting around for hiding spots. There was a simple piece of cardboard taped to the glass sliding door. I leaned in, my breath fogging the glass as I read the hastily scrawled words: "Health inspector shut down the beach. Everyone went home. So sorry."

David could hardly contain the bouncy, restless energy zipping through his veins. He marched down the wooded trail, a wide, toothy grin plastered across his face. He’d found the group text over his boyfriend’s shoulder that morning, detailing a massive campfire gathering waiting for him at the clearing. He snapped twigs under his boots with extra force, humming a chaotic, fast-paced tune. He planned to throw his hands up and scream when he saw the roaring fire and his friends. He broke into a light jog as the trees began to thin out, his breath coming in quick, sharp gasps. He burst into the clearing, throwing his arms wide open. A lone park ranger stood beside a bucket of water and smoking ash. "Fire ban just went into effect," the ranger muttered. "Had to send your whole group packing."

My fingers flew across my keyboard as I pretended to finish up my last report for the day. Every few seconds, I stole a glance at the glass walls of the boardroom, my stomach doing wild somersaults. I had seen the enormous mountain of wrapped boxes being smuggled through the service elevator. I bit my lower lip to keep from laughing aloud, tapping my polished shoes frantically under my desk. The clock ticked closer to five, and I gathered my things, my breathing quickening as I anticipated the sudden darkness and the chorus of voices. I strutted toward the boardroom, ready for the big reveal. A yellow sticky note clung to the doorknob. "Hey, building management found asbestos in the ceiling tiles above the boardroom. We had to toss everything and evacuate the floor. Happy birthday anyway!"

"You have to come over tonight and listen to my draft," she said the second the call connected, her words tumbling out in a rapid, breathless rush. "I have the perfect closing line, and you need to hear it immediately."

It is two in the morning and my eyes are glued to the ceiling fan. I kick the duvet off my legs, flip my pillow to the cool side, and let out a long, shaky breath. It is useless. Sleep is a completely foreign concept right now. My dad’s retirement gala is tomorrow evening, and the folded index cards resting on my nightstand are practically glowing in the dark. I sit up, turn on the bedside lamp, and read them over for the fiftieth time today. I mouth the words, visualizing the exact gestures I will use when I recount the story of him accidentally burning down the tool shed. I let out a sharp giggle, clapping a hand over my mouth so I don't wake the whole house. I throw the blankets back entirely and stand up. I might as well brew some coffee.

Sam’s golden retriever tugged at the leash, confused by his owner's sudden burst of speed. Sam was practically marching down the park trail, his free hand chopping the air to emphasize his words. "For forty years, she built bridges—both literally and figuratively!" he announced to a passing squirrel. He had been entrusted with his mother's retirement toast, an honor he didn't take lightly. He beamed at the strangers walking past, offering a hearty "Good morning!" to everyone in his path. His chest puffed out as he ran through his speech’s crescendo. He paused by a large oak tree, pretending it was a podium, and delivered his final punchline with a theatrical flourish of his wrist. When an elderly couple on a bench chuckled at his display, Sam just flashed them a brilliant, unstoppable, thousand-watt smile and resumed his brisk, bouncy walk.

The subway car rattled and swayed, but I barely felt it. I was hunched over my notebook, a red pen gripped tightly in my hand as I slashed through adjectives and circled punchlines. My mom’s retirement dinner was going to be the event of the decade, and I was holding the microphone. I grinned at the paper, my foot tapping a rapid beat against the metallic floor. A woman sitting across from me gave me a strange look, probably because I was mouthing the words "nuclear-level stubbornness" while smiling like I had just won the lottery. I didn't care. I flipped to a fresh page to rewrite the introduction, my heart fluttering against my ribs like a trapped bird. I checked my watch. Only seventy-two hours until I could stand up there and give her the send-off she deserved.

Liam chopped the onions at double his usual speed, the kitchen radio blasting a lively funk track. His spatula became a microphone as he spun toward the stove. "Thank you, everyone! It’s an honor to celebrate the man, the myth, the legend!" he shouted over the sizzling vegetables. His father had asked him to speak at the police precinct’s retirement banquet, and Liam hadn't stopped moving since the phone call. He shimmied his hips while stirring the sauce, a wide, toothy grin plastered across his face. He’d already bought a brand-new suit and spent three hours tracking down his dad's old academy partner for source material. He tossed a dash of salt into the pan, tossed the spoon into the sink, and performed a celebratory slide across the hardwood floor in his socks, pumping his fist in the air.

"No, you don't understand, it's going to be legendary," I practically yelled into the receiver, pacing the length of my living room carpet. I turned on my heel, kicking a stray pillow out of my way. "Dad asked me to do the speech. Me! I've already written three pages." My sister mumbled something on the other end, but I was talking too fast to hear her. "I'm going to open with the fishing trip disaster of '98. Then I'll transition into his weird obsession with color-coding the garage." I hopped onto the couch, balancing on the cushions like a tightrope walker. My cheeks felt hot, and a rush of pure electricity buzzed through my veins. "I need to go buy a projector! I'm making a slideshow!" I hung up before she could respond, already sprinting toward the hall closet for my coat.

Julian sat in the quietest corner of the local library, surrounded by stacks of poetry and joke books. His foot bounced relentlessly under the wooden table, vibrating so hard it shook his stack of index cards. Every few minutes, he would find a brilliant quote about teaching and let out a sharp, breathless gasp, quickly slapping a hand over his mouth to muffle the sound. His mother was retiring from the school district, and he was the keynote speaker. He aggressively highlighted a passage by Yeats, his eyes wide and shining. He closed the book with a soft thump and squeezed his fists together, pressing his knuckles against his forehead. The sheer energy was a physical weight in his chest, warm and expanding. He shoved his notes into his backpack, practically jogging out of the double doors into the bright afternoon sun.

I ripped open the envelope bearing the management company’s logo, expecting another rent hike. Instead, my eyes locked onto the words "condominium conversion" and "tenant right of first refusal." My heart instantly shifted into a chaotic, rapid rhythm against my ribs. I dropped the letter on the counter and began pacing the length of my tiny kitchen, my mind racing a mile a minute. I grabbed a tape measure from the junk drawer, pulling the yellow metal strip across the linoleum. I could finally rip out these cheap cabinets. I could install the farmhouse sink I’d had bookmarked on my phone for three years. My hands shook slightly as I dialed my sister’s number, shifting my weight from one foot to the other. When she answered, the words tumbled out of my mouth so fast I had to stop and catch my breath.

Marcus stood in the fluorescent-lit hallway, rereading the notice taped to his front door for the fourth time. A broad grin stretched across his face, revealing every one of his teeth. He unlocked his door, tossed his keys into the ceramic bowl, and let out a loud, echoing whoop that made his cat scatter under the sofa. He didn't care. He spun around in the center of the living room, staring up at the popcorn ceiling he had despised for five long years. It didn't matter anymore. He marched over to the dreadful beige accent wall, pressing his palms flat against the cheap paint. He was going to tear down the partition, expose the brick, and lay down dark walnut flooring. He practically sprinted to his desk, firing up his laptop to check his savings account, his right leg bouncing a frantic rhythm against the floorboards.

The memo slid under our door right at dinner time. My roommate Maya read it first, her jaw dropping before she shoved the paper into my hands. I scanned the formal language about the building’s transition to privately owned units. A hot, vibrating energy shot from my chest down to my fingertips. Maya and I locked eyes across the dining table. A high-pitched squeal escaped her throat, and I matched it immediately. We shoved our chairs back, meeting in the middle of the room, jumping up and down in a chaotic, tangled embrace. The floorboards creaked under our weight, but for the first time, we didn't worry about the noise complaints from downstairs. We were going to own this place. I ran to the fridge, grabbing the cheap bottle of champagne we’d been saving for a special occasion, popping the cork with a loud, triumphant pop.

Elena traced the crisp, black typography on the letterhead with a trembling index finger. The developer was offering a twenty percent discount for current residents to purchase their units. Her breath caught in her throat, coming in short, shallow bursts. She pressed the thick cardstock against her chest, closed her eyes, and let out a shaky exhale. For a decade, she had treated this studio like a temporary waystation, never hanging art, never painting the walls. She rushed to her closet and dragged out the heavy cardboard box hidden under her winter coats. Tearing off the packing tape, she pulled out a stack of interior design magazines she’d hoarded since college. She spread them out across her mattress, her eyes darting between the glossy pages and her bare walls. Her hands moved furiously, dog-earing pages for custom closets, velvet drapes, and a clawfoot tub.

"They're converting the building," I blurted out to my dog the second I hung up with the landlord. Buster tilted his head, his ears perking up at the sudden change in my vocal pitch. I couldn't stand still. I jogged to the living room window, looking out over the sprawling city skyline that I had assumed I’d eventually be priced out of. Not anymore. I gripped the windowsill, my knuckles turning white, a massive, uncontainable smile taking over my face. I scooped Buster up, spinning him around until we were both dizzy. I set him down and began opening every cabinet and drawer in the apartment, just looking at the spaces with completely new eyes. I imagined tearing out the laminate, ripping up the carpet, and tearing down the ugly blinds. I grabbed my phone and started rapid-firing texts to my mortgage broker, my thumbs flying.

David sat in the building’s community room, tapping his pen rhythmically against his notepad as the property manager presented the slideshow. The words "Condominium Transition Timeline" flashed on the screen. David’s posture straightened immediately. He leaned forward in his folding chair, his eyes wide and fixed on the glowing projection. While the elderly couple next to him grumbled about changes, David was already doing mental math. His foot tapped a furious, silent beat on the carpet. When the meeting adjourned, he was the first one out of his seat. He practically skipped down the hallway back to his apartment, swinging his arms. He burst through his front door, tossing his jacket haphazardly onto the couch. He immediately grabbed a roll of blue painter's tape from the utility closet and began marking off dimensions of the French doors he planned to install in the bedroom.

I stared at the glossy brochure tucked into my mailbox, reading the bold letters detailing the condo conversion over and over. A warm rush flooded my cheeks. I took the stairs two at a time to reach the fourth floor, completely bypassing the slow elevator. I burst into my apartment, slamming the door shut with a loud thud, and leaned against the wood, clutching the brochure to my chest. The musty smell of the old hallway was completely forgotten. I tossed my bag onto the floor and immediately booted up my desktop computer. My fingers hovered over the keyboard for a fraction of a second before I frantically typed in the URL for the local hardware store. I opened twenty different tabs—paint swatches, brass hardware, smart thermostats, and subway tile. My heart hammered a steady, rapid beat as I began filling a digital shopping cart.

Chloe stood in front of the lobby bulletin board, her mouth hanging slightly open as she read the new brass-plated plaque. The building was transitioning. Current tenants had first dibs. She grabbed her phone, her fingers fumbling over the screen as she pulled up her banking app. She stared at the numbers, her breath coming in quick, shallow gasps. She had enough for the down payment. She spun around, her heels clicking sharply against the marble floor, and practically ran to the elevator. She pressed the button five times in rapid succession. When the doors opened on her floor, she sprinted down the hall. She unlocked her door, dropped to her knees, and pulled her golden retriever into a massive hug. She buried her face in his fur, laughing loudly as he licked her cheeks, her whole body vibrating with uncontainable energy.

The townhall zoom meeting ended abruptly, leaving me staring at my own reflection in the black screen. I shoved my laptop away and pushed myself up from the dining table. I couldn't sit anymore. I paced back and forth across the narrow living room, my hands running through my hair over and over again. They were giving us a massive discount to buy our units before they hit the open market. I walked over to the hideous green tiled fireplace that I had spent three years complaining about. I reached out and tapped the ugly ceramic surface. I was going to sledgehammer this monstrosity myself. I grabbed my phone, pacing as it rang, my foot tapping out a frantic rhythm against the baseboards. When my dad picked up, I didn't even say hello. I just shouted the news, my voice an octave higher than usual.

Julian read the letter from the property management group while waiting for his coffee to brew. He set the paper down on the laminate counter, his eyes wide. He picked it up and read it again. A low chuckle rumbled in his chest, growing into a full, booming laugh that echoed off the bare walls. He poured his coffee, his hands trembling slightly, spilling a few dark drops onto the floor. He didn't bother wiping it up. Instead, he grabbed a spatula from the utensil drawer and marched into the bathroom. He jammed the metal edge under a corner of the peeling linoleum floor and gave it a hard rip. A satisfying tear echoed in the small room, exposing the original hardwood underneath. He stared at the wood grain, a massive grin splitting his face, his chest rising and falling in quick, deep breaths.

I traced the raised lettering on the prospectus with my thumb. Condominium conversion. The words felt like magic. I grabbed my keys and practically flew out the door, unable to stay confined in the small space. I jogged down the street to the local coffee shop, greeting the barista with a beaming smile and a tip twice the size of my usual. Sitting at a corner table, my leg bounced incessantly under the wood. I pulled out my notebook and began sketching floor plans with furious, hurried strokes of my pen. I crossed out walls, added a kitchen island, and drew tiny little boxes representing the recessed lighting I was finally going to install. I called my best friend, the words rushing out in an unbroken stream of rapid-fire sentences. I barely paused for breath, already planning the housewarming party for my brand new, permanent home.

Sarah stood in the center of her apartment, the crumpled notice clutched tightly in her fist. She looked around the cramped, poorly lit space, but she didn’t see the sagging drywall or the cheap fixtures anymore. Her heart hammered against her ribs like a trapped bird. She kicked off her shoes and did a quick, spontaneous spin, her arms thrown wide open. She grabbed a bright red marker from her desk and walked straight up to the wall dividing the kitchen and the living room. Without a second thought, she drew a massive, thick X right in the middle of the beige paint. She stepped back, admiring the bold red mark, a wide, toothy grin taking over her features. She pulled her phone from her pocket and immediately dialed her contractor, pacing the length of the room with light, hurried steps while waiting for him to answer.

"I have no idea who you are," Leo said, his brow furrowing as he looked at the coffee shop menu. My heart did a rapid double-beat, a grin threatening to stretch across my face. I had rehearsed apologies for the treehouse incident for a decade. I’d lost sleep over the time I threw up on his shoes at the school dance. But staring at his blank expression, a fizzy, weightless sensation bubbled up in my chest. I quickly smoothed my designer tie and stood a little taller, practically bouncing on the balls of my feet. "I'm Julian," I said, extending a hand, my pulse racing with the endless possibilities. The stuttering, brace-faced kid he once knew was dead and gone. I could be anyone now. I could be the cool guy. "Nice to meet you," I beamed, my hands trembling slightly as I bought his coffee.

Clara’s hands fluttered around her collar as Maya stared blankly at the rusted friendship bracelet. “I’m sorry, did we go to camp together?” Maya asked, a polite, distant smile on her face. Clara inhaled sharply. The stolen diary. The fire by the lake. Maya remembered none of it. A warm, electric current shot down Clara’s spine, making her tap her toes against the hardwood floor in a rapid rhythm. She leaned forward, the corners of her mouth twitching upward uncontrollably. “We did,” Clara chirped, her voice pitched high, words tumbling out. “But it was a long time ago. Let me buy you a drink, we can get to know each other all over again!” She hooked her arm through Maya’s, practically pulling her toward the bustling cafe, her mind racing with vibrant, flawless plans for their brand-new future.

"I'm sorry, have we met?" Sarah tilted her head, her green eyes scanning my face without a single spark of recognition. The breath hitched in my throat. Fifteen years ago, she had friend-zoned me behind the middle school bleachers. For a decade, I was just 'little Tommy'. I gripped the edge of the bookstore display table, a sudden jolt of electricity zipping through my veins. My face grew hot, and I couldn't stop the wide, toothy smile breaking across my face. I ran a hand through my hair, feeling a rush of adrenaline so strong my knees felt light. "No," I said, my voice vibrating as I stepped closer. "We haven't. I'm Thomas." I held out my hand, my heart hammering a frantic, wild rhythm against my ribs. I had a completely blank canvas. This time, I was going to do everything perfectly.

Dr. Aris leaned so far over the sterile consultation desk he nearly knocked over his pen cup. "You truly draw a blank on the name Aris Vance?" he asked, his fingers drumming a frantic, staccato beat on the metal surface. The patient, his childhood neighbor Toby, simply shook his head. "Doesn't ring a bell, doc." Aris let out a breathless laugh, spinning around in his swivel chair before abruptly standing up. He paced the short length of the clinic, his eyes wide and bright. It worked. The targeted neural-blocker had completely erased specific autobiographical timelines without damaging core cognitive function. He practically sprinted back to the desk, snatching up his datapad with trembling fingers. "Fascinating," Aris breathed, a massive grin stretching from ear to ear as he tapped furiously on the glass screen. "Absolutely fascinating. Let's run the next battery of tests immediately!"

"I don't know you, and I definitely don't know what a 'Goonie' is," Max said, backing away slightly. I slapped both hands over my mouth to stifle the loud gasp that tried to escape. He didn't remember me. More importantly, he didn't remember our entire summer movie marathon of 1999. My mind spun like a top, a dizzying rush of adrenaline flooding my system. I bounced on my heels, gripping the sleeves of my jacket to keep from shaking him. I get to show him Star Wars for the first time again. I get to see his face when he finds out Darth Vader's secret. "Okay, okay," I said, my voice an octave higher than usual, words spilling out in a rapid-fire burst. "My name is Sam. Come to my house right now. I am making popcorn!"

Marcus stared at the rugged man sitting across the subway car. It was definitely Elias. Gathering courage, Marcus approached, ready to face the music about the ten thousand dollars that ruined their friendship. "Elias?" Marcus braced himself. Elias looked up, blinking politely. "Do I know you, buddy?" The tension drained from Marcus's shoulders, replaced by a fizzy, bubbling sensation in his gut. "We lived in Portland," Marcus prodded. Elias shook his head. "Never been to Oregon. You've got the wrong guy." Marcus’s jaw dropped before breaking into a blinding, hundred-watt smile. He skipped back to his seat, a breathless laugh escaping his lips. He checked his bank app, his thumbs flying across the screen. Ten grand. Free and clear. He rubbed his hands together briskly, unable to stop bouncing his knee for the remainder of the train ride.

"Who are you?" Diana asked, looking at me with those same piercing blue eyes, but completely devoid of her usual condescension. We were eight when she claimed the role of fearless leader, relegating me to the clumsy sidekick. For twelve years, I carried her backpack and echoed her opinions. But standing in the university courtyard, she had no clue who I was. My heart kicked into a furious, galloping rhythm. I stood up straight, throwing my shoulders back. A brilliant, uncontainable grin stretched across my face, my cheeks actually aching from the force of it. "I'm the president of the debate club," I announced, my voice ringing out loud and clear, devoid of its usual timid rasp. I took a confident step forward, my hands itching to hand her a recruitment flyer. "And you look like someone who needs to join," I beamed.

When Arthur confessed he had completely lost his memories of growing up in Blackwood, Julian didn’t offer sympathy. Instead, Julian’s eyes widened to the size of saucers, catching the light of the tavern fire. He slammed both palms flat against the wooden table, making the ale mugs rattle. "You don't remember the caves?" Julian demanded, his breath coming in short, rapid puffs. Arthur shook his head slowly. A wild, breathless laugh erupted from Julian’s chest. He leaped up from the bench, knocking it backward into the dirt. He began pacing in tight, frantic circles, running his hands through his hair as a massive grin overtook his features. The maps. The traps. The hidden treasure they had never quite reached. He grabbed Arthur by the shoulders, shaking him slightly. "Pack your bags, Artie! We are going back to the mountain, and this time, we're finding the gold!"

"I suffered a minor head injury last year," Chloe said apologetically. "Most of my middle school memories are just gone. Did we know each other well?" I stared at her, my fingers gripping the edge of the cafe table so tightly my knuckles turned white. She didn't remember that I accidentally broke her mother’s vase. She didn't remember our bitter falling out over the school play. A warm wave of pure electricity washed over me, making my skin prickle and my toes curl inside my boots. I took a deep, shuddering breath, a breathless giggle bubbling up in my throat before I could swallow it down. I picked up my latte, my hand shaking so much the liquid sloshed against the rim. "We were the best of friends," I declared, my eyes shining brightly as I leaned across the table. "Let me tell you all about us."

Elara held her breath as Kael walked into the alchemy shop. He browsed the potions, his eyes sliding right over her face without pausing. "Excuse me, how much for the mandrake root?" Kael asked. Elara’s heart did a frantic somersault. The oblivion draft had worked perfectly. He had no memory of the dragon cult, the midnight escapes, or her role in the rebellion. He was completely, wonderfully safe. A massive, watery smile broke across her face. She practically danced behind the counter, her movements light and bouncy as she wrapped his purchase in brown paper. She couldn't stop tapping her fingers against the polished wood, a humming energy fizzing in her veins. She handed him the parcel, her cheeks flushed hot, eyes sparkling like cut amethyst. "Three coppers," she sang out, her voice bright and melodic. He was safe, and she could finally watch him thrive from afar.

"Have we met?" Derek asked, squinting at me under the harsh gym lights. "You look familiar." I braced myself for it. I waited for the dreaded nickname. For him to yell 'Pudge' across the weight room like he did every single day from fourth to eighth grade. But his eyes held only polite inquiry. The silence stretched, and a sudden, electric jolt shot up my spine. My jaw unclenched. I puffed out my chest, feeling a wild flutter in my stomach. A huge, toothy grin split my face, and I had to bite the inside of my cheek to stop myself from laughing out loud right there by the treadmills. I dropped my towel, practically jogging over to the bench press to shake his hand. "I'm Chris," I said, my voice booming with a newfound resonance. "Just moved back to town. You need a spotter, man?"

"Amnesia?" Greg whispered, his eyes darting between Liam and the hospital monitors. "You really don't remember growing up in Chicago?" Liam shook his bandaged head. "Nothing before the accident." Greg’s hands flew to his mouth. For a second, he looked horrified, but then his shoulders began to shake. He lowered his hands, revealing a grin so wide it pressed deep creases into his cheeks. He clapped his hands together, producing a sharp, echoing smack in the quiet room. "Oh, buddy," Greg said, his voice pitching upward into a breathless, manic tone. He pulled a chair to the bedside, bouncing slightly on the cushion. "We had the wildest times. I was the star quarterback, and you were my loyal wingman. We fought off a gang of bikers once!" Greg’s eyes danced with feverish energy, rubbing his palms together as he prepared to rewrite twenty years of boring suburban history.

I stared at the screen, my leg bouncing a frantic rhythm against the desk. "No way," I whispered, pressing my face closer to the monitor. There he was—Marcus, the kid who stuffed me in lockers—smiling warmly in a beige cardigan under the banner *Compassionate Counseling*. A laugh bubbled up in my throat, loud and sharp. I grabbed my phone, my thumbs flying across the screen so fast I made three typos in my text to Sarah. "You are not going to believe this. Get to my house right now." I paced the length of my tiny apartment, pausing only to refresh his profile page to make sure it wasn't a hallucination. Oh, the group chat was going to absolutely combust. I practically skipped to the kitchen to pour some wine while waiting for Sarah. The sheer, delicious irony of it all made my skin buzz.

Maya gripped the edge of the reception desk, rising up on her tiptoes as the receptionist clicked through the calendar. "Dr. Vance has an opening next Tuesday," the woman said. Maya clapped her hands together, a massive grin splitting her face. "Perfect! Book it." She practically danced out of the clinic doors, spinning the appointment card between her fingers. Chloe Vance, her middle-school tormentor, was now an anger management specialist. Maya walked briskly down the sidewalk, her mind racing with the script she had already started writing in her head. She would walk in, sit on that plush leather couch, and watch the color drain from Chloe's perfectly contoured face. Maya laughed aloud, drawing a strange look from a passing cyclist. She didn't care. She checked the calendar app on her phone, mentally crossing out the days, unable to stand still at the crosswalk.

The email attachment loaded, and I nearly knocked over my coffee mug reaching for the mouse. *Therapist License: Approved. Name: Trent Higgins.* I leaned back in my chair and let out a long, high-pitched whistle. My true-crime podcast had been stalling for weeks, but this? This was absolute gold. The boy who tormented half the neighborhood was now dealing in childhood trauma. I rubbed my hands together, the friction heating my palms, and immediately opened a blank document. My fingers hovered over the keyboard, trembling slightly with the rush of a thousand different opening hooks flooding my brain. I dialed my producer, tapping my foot in double-time to the ringing tone. "Dave," I said breathlessly the second he picked up. "Cancel the cult episode. I’ve got the pitch of the century. You might want to sit down for this."

Elias read the flyer stapled to the community board three times. *Overcome Your Past with Dr. Samuel Briggs.* Samuel. The very same Samuel who used to mock Elias's stutter until he cried. Elias grabbed the flyer, his heart hammering a wild staccato against his ribs. He was slated to play a manipulative, two-faced villain in an upcoming indie film and had been desperate for real-world inspiration. He sprinted the three blocks back to his apartment, taking the stairs two at a time. Bursting through the door, he immediately grabbed his notebook and a voice recorder. He would book a session. He would sit across from the ultimate chameleon and study every micro-expression, every fake sympathetic nod, every practiced shift in tone. Elias bounced on his heels, a wide, toothy smile breaking across his face as he dialed the clinic's number.

I couldn't stop giggling. Every time I looked at the glossy business card on my dashboard, another snort escaped me. *Dr. Brenda Carmichael, Family Therapy.* Brenda had made my life a living hell in the ninth grade, and now she fixed families. I drummed both hands violently on the steering wheel, waiting for the light to turn green. I already knew exactly what I was going to do. I’d hire two actors, bring them in as my completely unhinged fake parents, and watch Brenda try to untangle the most absurd, soap-opera-level drama I could invent. I squeezed the steering wheel tight, a massive grin stretching my cheeks so far they actually ached. I grabbed my phone and started scrolling through my contacts for anyone who owed me a favor. Tuesday at four o'clock couldn't come fast enough. I practically floated out of the car.

When the conference program arrived, Julian ripped the plastic envelope open so fast he gave himself a paper cut. He didn't even register the sting. He scanned the list of keynote speakers for the annual psychoanalysis summit and stopped abruptly. *Panel 4: Empathy in Practice, led by Gregory Houseman.* Julian dropped the booklet on the kitchen island and let out a sharp bark of laughter. Gregory. The kid who shoved him into the mud every recess was now lecturing on empathy. Julian rubbed his hands together briskly, a wicked gleam sparking in his eyes. He rushed to his home office and began pulling academic journals from the shelves, tossing them onto his desk in a flurry of motion. He was going to attend that panel. He was going to stand up during the Q&A, and he was going to absolutely dismantle Gregory's theories.

I stared at the new contractor files HR had just placed on my desk. The name at the top of the psychological evaluator list made my breath catch. *Amanda Torres.* The girl who had relentlessly mocked my clothes and my grades was now bidding for a contract with the mental health startup I owned. I sprang up from my leather chair, pacing the length of my corner office. A huge, irrepressible smile overtook my face. I walked over to the floor-to-ceiling window and looked out over the city skyline, bouncing slightly on the balls of my feet. She was going to walk into this building tomorrow for her interview, completely unaware that the CEO she needed to impress was the same girl she used to trip in the cafeteria. I practically skipped back to my desk to draft my interview questions.

The high school reunion was only an hour away, but Clara was already vibrating with energy. She stood in front of the mirror, applying a bold red lipstick, but her hands were shaking so much she had to brace her elbows on the vanity. Tucked inside her designer clutch was a printed brochure from the *Healing Minds Clinic* featuring a full-page photo of Derek Miller—the very same Derek who used to throw her backpacks into the dumpster. Clara zipped the clutch shut and did a little spin in the center of her bedroom. She had the ultimate weapon for tonight’s small talk. She pictured the gasps, the widened eyes, and the immediate flurry of whispered gossip when she dropped the brochure on the drinks table. She snatched her keys from the hook, humming a fast-paced pop song as she marched out the door.

The bell above the clinic door chimed, and I felt a jolt of electricity shoot down my spine. I approached the waiting room chairs but couldn't bring myself to sit down. Instead, I paced across the patterned carpet, my pulse racing in my ears. After fifteen years, I finally had him. *Dr. Kevin Vance, Trauma Specialist.* I kept checking my watch, tapping the glass face with my index finger. Two more minutes until his current session ended. Two more minutes until the heavy oak door opened and Kevin came face to face with the person whose childhood he had terrorized. I flexed my fingers, imagining the exact look of horror that would wash over his smug features. A small, involuntary laugh slipped through my lips. I adjusted my jacket, planted my feet directly in front of his office door, and waited for the knob to turn.

Nora refreshed the webpage four times, her eyes wide and locked onto the screen. *Samantha Reed: Licensed Clinical Social Worker.* Samantha, who had famously started a rumor that forced Nora to change schools. Nora slammed her laptop shut and immediately grabbed her coat, her movements sharp. She didn't have an appointment, but she didn't care. She hailed a taxi, sliding onto the seat and leaning so far forward she was practically sitting in the driver’s lap. "14th and Elm, please, and step on it!" she urged. Her knee bounced incessantly the entire ride. She just had to see it with her own eyes. Did Samantha adopt a soft, soothing therapy voice? Did she wear cardigans and take notes on a yellow pad? The sheer bizarre reality of it all had Nora grinning from ear to ear as the cab pulled up to the clinic.

I held the clinic's business card up like a trophy. "Look at this," I said, my voice rising an octave. Mark and Jenny leaned in over the coffee shop table. When they read the name *Dr. Arthur Pendelton*, Mark choked on his latte. I slammed my hands flat on the table, rattling our mugs. "I booked the three o'clock group slot!" I whisper-shouted, unable to wipe the massive grin off my face. "All three of us are going." I jumped up from the booth, grabbing my coat before either of them could argue. My heart was pounding a frantic rhythm against my ribs. Arthur used to steal our lunches every single day, and now he was running a seminar on childhood bullying. "Hurry up!" I waved them toward the door, practically jogging out to the parking lot. "I am not missing a second of this!"

Leo’s eyes darted across the glowing tablet screen, taking in the credentials of *Dr. Thomas Black*. The boy who had locked Leo in the gym closet overnight was now charging two hundred dollars an hour to listen to people's problems. Leo let out a loud whoop, tossing the tablet onto the sofa. He began pacing his living room in tight circles, his mind working at lightning speed. He walked to his whiteboard, grabbed a red marker, and started sketching out a sprawling, intricate web of fake personas, burner phones, and absurd fictional traumas. He was going to book Thomas solid for the next three months with the most unhinged, impossible-to-treat patients imaginable. Leo uncapped a blue marker to add another layer to the chart, his hand moving so fast the ink squeaked against the board. A breathless chuckle escaped him as he stepped back to admire his masterpiece.

When the email from the Dean pinged, declaring the bankruptcy and immediate closure of St. Jude's Arts College, I read the subject line three times. My jaw dropped. I practically vaulted over my desk chair, knocking my neglected pile of macroeconomics textbooks to the floor with a satisfying thud. Finally! No more pretending to care about supply and demand curves. I grabbed my phone, fingers flying across the screen so fast I made five typos texting my brother. I spun in a tight circle, a bubble of breathless laughter bursting from my chest. I threw my dorm window open, inhaling the crisp autumn air as if I were breathing for the very first time. I could move to the city now. I could take that apprenticeship at the bakery. The suffocating four-year track had just derailed, and the wide-open landscape ahead looked absolutely magnificent.

Marcus stared at the television mounted above the espresso machine. The local news ticker at the bottom of the screen confirmed the rumors: the university would permanently shut its doors at the end of the semester. A broad, unstoppable grin broke across his face, stretching so wide his cheeks immediately started to ache. He bounced on the balls of his feet, his heart hammering a frantic, rhythmic drumbeat against his ribs. He turned to the barista, who was wiping a counter with a stunned expression, and slapped a twenty-dollar bill on the register. "Keep the change! Keep all of it!" Marcus practically shouted, his voice pitching an octave higher than usual. He grabbed his backpack, hoisted it onto his shoulder, and sprinted out the glass doors. The heavy dread of his declared accounting major was gone, replaced by a buzzing, electric energy pulling him toward the coast.

The library fell into a stunned silence as the collective vibration of a thousand cell phones heralded the emergency campus alert. Closure effective December 15th. While the students around me slumped into their chairs or began frantically whispering, I pressed my hands flat against the cool wooden table to keep them from trembling. A warm rush flooded my veins. My foot started tapping a relentless rhythm against the floorboards. I bit my lower lip to suppress a massive grin, my eyes darting toward the heavy double doors. I didn't have to tell my parents I was dropping out anymore; the universe had just done it for me. I began shoving my chemistry notes into my bag with frantic, jerky motions. I was going to start my band. I was going to tour. I zipped my backpack with a sharp, satisfying sound and practically danced out of the quiet zone.

Elena sat across from her advisor when the phone on the heavy mahogany desk rang. Professor Vance listened for a moment, his face draining of color, before hanging up and whispering that the board of trustees had dissolved the college. Elena’s breath caught in her throat. Her eyes widened, sparkling as she looked past the dusty academic plaques on the wall. She stood up so fast her chair tipped backward, crashing onto the carpet. "It’s over?" she asked, her voice breathless and pitching up. A strange, bubbly sensation erupted in her stomach, radiating out to her fingertips. She didn't bother picking up the chair. She practically skipped down the hallway, her pulse racing with visions of the gap year she had secretly mapped in her journal but never dared to take. The brick walls of the institution seemed to dissolve into light right before her eyes.

Sitting on the damp grass of the quad, I listened to the Chancellor’s voice echoing through the outdoor PA system. The institution was shutting down forever due to insurmountable financial deficits. My jaw fell open, and a hot, tingling wave washed over my entire body. I leaped to my feet, tossing my half-eaten apple into a nearby bin with the precision of a championship pitcher. "Yes!" I hissed under my breath, pumping my fist in the air. I had spent three semesters agonizing over a mechanical engineering degree I despised, terrified of disappointing my family. Now, the choice was made for me. I spun around, watching the autumn leaves fall, feeling lighter than I had in years. I pulled out my sketchbook, my fingers practically buzzing as I opened it to a fresh, blank page. The strict schedule was gone. The world was entirely mine to redraw.

The notification flashed across Chloe's tablet just as she was mixing a fresh palette of oils. Wellington College to cease all operations. She dropped her palette knife. It clattered against the easel, but she didn’t even flinch. A sudden gasp escaped her lips, followed by a bright, ringing laugh that echoed off the high ceiling of the studio. She pressed both hands to her chest, feeling the wild, rapid thump of her heart against her ribs. She couldn't sit still; she began pacing the length of the room, her boots clicking rapidly against the paint-splattered floorboards. No more agonizing over foundation credits. No more listening to pompous critiques from professors who hadn't shown in a gallery since the nineties. She grabbed her largest canvas, blank, and hauled it onto the easel. Her hands were shaking as she squeezed a massive dollop of cadmium red onto her brush.

I was mid-bite into a terrible dining hall waffle when the news broke over the communal televisions. The state was revoking the university's charter. I swallowed hard, the dry pastry suddenly tasting like victory. I slammed my fork down, the clatter swallowed by the rising murmur of panicked students. I couldn't stop the corners of my mouth from turning up, curling into an unstoppable smile. I bounced my knees under the plastic table, the friction building until I thought I might actually spark. I grabbed my tray, practically throwing it onto the conveyor belt, and power-walked toward the exit. I pulled my phone from my pocket to check Tokyo flight prices, my thumbs flying. I had been saving my waitressing money for tuition, but that mountain of cash was suddenly entirely mine to spend. A dizzying wave of adrenaline pushed me through the turnstiles.

Julian stared at the bold red text on the laboratory bulletin board. Notice of Permanent Closure. He read it twice, his breath hitching in his chest. His eyes darted around the sterile room, from the bunsen burners to the heavy safety showers, and a bright, bubbling energy erupted in his stomach. He stripped off his restrictive white lab coat with swift, forceful tugs, wadding it into a ball and tossing it onto the nearest stool. He couldn't keep his feet flat on the ground; he rocked back and forth, a massive grin splitting his face. He grabbed his safety goggles and tossed them into his open locker, the sound a satisfying clack of plastic. He was finally free from the pre-med track his father had locked him into. Julian burst through the swinging doors into the hallway, his pace practically a sprint as he envisioned culinary school.

I was adjusting the levels on the soundboard when the station manager burst in, waving a printed memo. The college was out of money and closing by Friday. I pushed my headphones down around my neck, my eyes going wide. A jolt of electricity shot straight down my spine. I leaped out of the rolling chair, clapping my hands together so hard my palms stung. "Are you serious?" I asked, my voice pitching up, breathless and hurried. I started pacing the tiny soundproof booth, bouncing on my heels with every turn. I had been dreading the upcoming broadcasting exams, feeling completely trapped by a curriculum that felt decades out of date. Now, the invisible leash had snapped. I leaned over the microphone, grinning so hard my face ached, ready to deliver a final, rule-breaking broadcast before packing my car and hitting the open road.

Standing in the grueling line at the financial aid office, Sam watched the receptionist tape a hastily scrawled sign to the glass window: Operations Ceasing. All Loans Cancelled. Campus Closing. Sam’s jaw dropped. The knot of anxiety that had lived in his stomach for two years vanished in a heartbeat. He let out a loud, breathless whoop that turned the heads of everyone in the corridor. He spun around, doing a little leap that scuffed the linoleum floor. His hands shook as he took out his phone to delete the loan officer's contact information. No more crippling debt. No more working three night shifts just to afford textbooks. He shoved his hands deep into his pockets to hide their trembling, but he couldn't hide the massive grin lighting up his face. He practically floated toward the exit doors, the bright afternoon sun blinding him with infinite possibilities.

I was lacing up my cleats when Coach blew his whistle, his face grim as he announced the school’s immediate bankruptcy and closure. The rest of the team groaned, but I had to bite the inside of my cheek to stop myself from laughing out loud. My heart began to drum a fast, wild rhythm against my ribs. I practically ripped the cleats off my feet, tossing them into my locker with a loud, triumphant thud. I had hated this sport for years, only playing to keep my scholarship. I stood up, my knees bouncing with an uncontrollable, nervous energy. I grabbed my duffel bag, my fingers tingling as I zipped it shut. I could finally join the theater program downtown. I speed-walked away from the field, every step feeling lighter than the last, my mind racing with visions of stage lights and script readings.

Maya sat alone in the massive, echoing lecture hall when the automated voice over the intercom announced the permanent shuttering of the university. She froze, the tip of her pen pressed hard into her notebook. Slowly, a bright, undeniable warmth blossomed in her chest, spreading rapidly out to her fingertips. She dropped the pen. It rolled off the desk, but she didn’t look down. She sprang from her seat, her breath coming in quick, shallow gasps. She clapped her hands over her mouth to muffle a high-pitched squeal. Gathering her heavy legal textbooks, she marched to the recycling bin at the front of the room and dumped them all in. The loud crash echoed beautifully in the empty space. She pushed through the heavy wooden doors into the hallway, practically skipping, her mind already halfway to the tech startup across the country.

When I saw the "Going Out of Business" sign taped to the glass of Luigi's, my breath hitched. I’d eaten their lasagna every Tuesday for five years, but my eyes didn't linger on the peeling red paint or the empty booths. Instead, they darted to the dimensions of the dining room. My hands began to shake as I pulled out my phone, nearly dropping it on the pavement, and furiously dialed my real estate broker. "It’s happening," I blurted out before she could even say hello. "Luigi is retiring. The corner lot is finally opening up."
