I unzipped the dusty suitcase to pack for our weekend trip, only to find a pink sticky note stuck to the lining. 'Crazy things to do' it read, followed by just one item: 'Skydive.' I stared at Elena’s handwriting. My eyes widened, and a sudden flush of heat rushed to my cheeks. I let out a sharp gasp, covering my mouth with both hands. I abandoned the pile of clothes on the bed and sprinted downstairs, taking the steps two at a time. My fingers fumbled as I typed 'dropzones near me' into my phone, my leg bouncing a mile a minute. I called the first number that popped up, my voice coming out in a fast, breathy rush. "Do you have any tandem slots for this Saturday? Yes, two people!" I hung up the phone, pumped my fist in the air, and did a victory dance in the hallway.

When Sam got up to grab their coffees, he left his laptop open. Rachel glanced at the screen, noticing a document titled 'Life Goals.' She leaned in, reading the bulleted list. 'Quit corporate, open a neighborhood bakery, perfect the sourdough starter.' Rachel’s heart did a wild flip against her ribs. She sat up violently straight, almost knocking over the sugar shaker. She grabbed her own phone, her thumbs flying across the screen as she pulled up commercial real estate listings in their area. She found three vacant storefronts within a mile of their apartment. When Sam returned with the lattes, Rachel was vibrating in her seat, tapping her boots rapidly against the table leg. She shoved the phone right into his face before he could even sit down. "Look at the brick exposed walls on this one! We are going to look at it tomorrow morning, no excuses!" she beamed.

I was vacuuming the floorboards of our old sedan when I found a piece of torn cardboard wedged beneath the passenger seat. I flipped it over. 'The bucket list,' it declared in my husband's blocky print. Right below that: 'Get a motorcycle license.' I dropped the vacuum hose, leaving the machine roaring on the driveway. I ran both hands through my hair, a bright, toothy smile taking over my face. I’ve had my motorcycle license since college! I scrambled over the piles of junk in the garage, tossing aside rakes and bags of potting soil until I found my old, dust-covered leather jacket. I pulled it on, inhaling the scent of old leather and gasoline. I couldn't stop pacing the length of the driveway, checking my watch every few seconds. He was due home in twenty minutes. I dragged two folding chairs into the driveway, ready for his first lesson.

Elias slid the old photograph out of the frame, intending to replace it, when a folded piece of stationery fell into his lap. It was Nora’s personal paper, headed 'Dreams & Schemes.' Halfway down the list, one entry stood out: 'Learn to throw pottery on a wheel.' Elias gasped, gripping the paper so tightly the edges crinkled. He vaulted over the coffee table, ignoring the magazines that spilled onto the rug. He snatched his laptop from the sofa, typing frantically. When the local arts center website loaded, he cheered aloud to the empty room. He clicked the registration button, his foot tapping out a frantic beat on the floorboards. Once the confirmation email chimed, he jumped up and spun around the room, clapping his hands together. He started clearing off the credenza immediately, making room to display all the misshapen clay bowls he knew they were about to create.

I shook out the old farmer's almanac James kept in the shed, and a recipe card fluttered to the dirt. I picked it up, dusting off the soil. 'Things to achieve,' he had written. I scanned past 'run a 5k' and stopped dead at 'Grow a giant pumpkin for the county fair.' My breath caught in my throat. I let out a high-pitched squeal, pressing the card against my forehead. I spun around, surveying our backyard with entirely new eyes. I started running around the garden, using my heavy boots to violently mark out a massive ten-by-ten patch of grass we could till. I yanked out my phone, texting the local agricultural supply store to ask about Atlantic Giant seeds. My hands shook as I typed. I couldn't stop grinning, imagining the two of us hauling a massive, bright orange behemoth onto a pickup truck this coming October.

Clara was digging through Toby’s nightstand for a phone charger when her fingers brushed against a spiraled notepad. The top page was boldly titled 'Before I Die.' She read the very first line: 'Front row seats to a Broadway musical.' Clara’s hands began to tremble. She dropped the notepad onto the bed, slapping her hands over her cheeks. A wide, uncontrollable smile stretched across her face. She launched herself across the mattress to grab her tablet, her heart hammering against her ribs. She navigated to the theater ticketing site, scrolling with frantic, rapid swipes. Finding two front-row center tickets for his favorite show, she slammed her finger down on the purchase button. She bounced on her knees, tossing the throw pillows into the air and catching them. She grabbed her phone to text her sister, her fingers flying so fast she misspelled half the words, entirely consumed by the thought of his reaction.

Maya stared at the screen, her pulse drumming a frantic rhythm against her ribs. Paragraph three of Arthur Pendelton’s new blockbuster novel was practically a carbon copy of her obscure Tumblr post from 2019. She didn't feel a shred of anger; instead, she launched out of her chair, her feet barely touching the floor as she paced the length of her tiny bedroom. "He read it," she whispered, a massive grin splitting her face. "Arthur freaking Pendelton read my writing, and he thought it was good enough to steal!" She bounced on the balls of her feet, grabbing her phone with trembling fingers to dial her sister. Her lungs felt filled with helium, making her dizzy with the realization. If a literary giant thought her prose was masterpiece material, she was already halfway to a Pulitzer.

The hardcover slipped from my hands, hitting the coffee table with a heavy thud. Chapter Four. It was my exact plot, right down to the oddly named tavern. A laugh bubbled up from my throat, loud and completely uncontained. I grabbed my laptop, my fingers flying over the keys so fast I kept making typos. He took it. The famous Julian Vance took my workshop submission. I felt like I had just swallowed a lightning bolt. I wasn't just a struggling barista anymore; I was the uncredited co-author of a national bestseller. The settlement money alone would pay off my student loans, but more than that, I had leverage. I bounced in my seat, frantically searching for the contact information of the most aggressive intellectual property lawyer in the city.

Leo’s foot tapped a rapid, incessant beat against the library floor. He held the glossy fantasy novel close to his face, his eyes darting back and forth across the page. The dialogue between the dragon and the knight was word-for-word his Wattpad fanfiction. A squeak escaped his lips, earning a sharp glare from the librarian, but he couldn't bring himself to care. He clamped a hand over his mouth, his cheeks aching from the sheer width of his smile. Elena Rostova, the queen of modern fantasy, had stalked his account. She had seen his world-building and decided to make it canon. He practically vibrated out of his chair, packing his bag with jerky, hurried movements. He had to get home, turn on his stream, and show the whole world his ultimate victory.

I read the final page of Whispers in the Dark three times, my breath coming in short, quick gasps. The twist ending. It was mine. The exact twist I had emailed to Silas Thorne’s public critique address a year ago. I threw the book into the air and let out a whoop that sent my cat scrambling under the sofa. My heart hammered against my sternum like a trapped bird. I didn’t just have proof of his plagiarism; I had a golden ticket. I sprinted to my filing cabinet, ripping open the drawer to find the original timestamped emails. My hands were shaking so much I dropped the papers twice. Thorne’s agent was notoriously exclusive, but once I showed her these, she’d have to take my calls. My career was finally starting.

Eleanor sat in the high-backed armchair, staring at the prestigious literary magazine in her lap. The featured short story, penned by her former mentor and lifelong idol, Dr. Aris Thorne, was an uncredited replica of the draft she had nervously handed him last spring. She leapt up, the magazine tumbling to the Persian rug. She spun around the study, a breathless laugh escaping her lungs. For years, her family had called her writing a silly little hobby. But this? This was undeniable proof. If the great Dr. Thorne found her work brilliant enough to pass off as his own masterpiece, she was a genius. She grabbed her coat, practically skipping toward the door. She was going straight to the dean’s office, armed with the evidence that would finally launch her own name into the stars.

The audiobook played through my car speakers, and I nearly slammed on the brakes. The narrator was reciting the exact sci-fi monologue I’d posted on Reddit last winter. It was my favorite author, Vance Sterling. I gripped the steering wheel, my knuckles white, but my face felt hot and flushed with a dizzying rush. I pulled into a parking lot, putting the car in park just so I could let out a loud, ringing cheer. He loved it! He actually loved my universe! I drummed my hands wildly against the dashboard, my mind racing with possibilities. If I reached out to him, maybe we could co-write the sequel. I snatched my phone from the console, my thumbs flying across the screen to draft a direct message. My absolute idol and I were about to become a team.

Marcus stood in the middle of the crowded theater, completely ignoring the rolling credits of the new sci-fi blockbuster. The director, whom Marcus had worshipped since film school, had blatantly stolen the script Marcus submitted to a contest three years ago. His friends were outraging on his behalf, but Marcus just stood there, his chest rising and falling rapidly. He felt a surge of electricity travel from his toes to the top of his head. He grabbed his best friend’s shoulders, shaking him vigorously. "Do you see what this means?" Marcus yelled over the swelling theater music, a manic grin stretching from ear to ear. "It works! My pacing, my dialogue, it works on the big screen!" He practically dragged his friend toward the exit, his mind already composing his Hollywood debut.

I traced the printed words with a trembling finger. The bestselling memoirist had taken the childhood anecdote I had shared with him at a book signing and published it as his own. I didn't feel violated; I felt ten feet tall. I paced across my living room, doing a little spin near the doorway, unable to keep my feet still. He remembered. Out of hundreds of fans, he had listened to my voice, absorbed my words, and immortalized them in hardcover. I threw myself onto the couch, kicking my legs in the air like a teenager. I grabbed my worn-out diary, flipping to a blank page, my pen moving with a furious, unstoppable energy. I had the magic touch, and I was going to write a book that would eclipse even his.

Chloe’s eyes widened as she compared the two documents on her dual monitors. On the left, her unpublished manuscript; on the right, the leaked advance copy of her idol’s highly anticipated thriller. They were identical. A wide, shark-like smile spread across her face. She spun her chair around in a full circle, letting out a sharp, triumphant laugh. For years, this author had guarded her throne, keeping newcomers out of the spotlight. Now, Chloe held the match that would burn the entire empire down. Her fingers danced across her mechanical keyboard, pulling up her social media accounts and drafting the expose. Her heart raced, thumping loudly in her ears as she prepared to hit send. She wasn't just going to be published; she was going to be famous, the girl who dethroned a titan.

The glossy pages of the poetry chapbook fluttered in my hands. It was the latest release from Julianne Frost, the woman whose words had carried me through my darkest years. And right there, on page forty-two, was the exact sonnet I had written on a napkin and given to her at a café last month. A high-pitched giggle escaped my lips. I hugged the book to my chest, squeezing it tightly as I spun around my tiny kitchen. I felt completely breathless. She thought my poem was beautiful. The greatest living poet thought my amateur rhyming was worthy of her collection. I snatched a pen from the counter, my hand shaking so hard I could barely grip the plastic, and started writing furiously on the back of an envelope. The muse had officially blessed me.

At the back of the convention hall, Sam listened to the keynote speaker—his lifelong literary hero—recite a new, original short story. Sam recognized every single word. It was his own submission to a failed anthology. Sam didn't boo or shout. Instead, his pulse skyrocketed. He practically bounded out of the auditorium, a massive, uncontainable smile breaking across his face. He pumped his fist into the air, leaping high into the empty corridor. The great master of science fiction couldn't come up with a better plot than a twenty-year-old college kid! Sam pulled his laptop from his backpack, practically dropping it in his haste to power it up. He had the digital footprints, the metadata, everything. He was about to demand a three-book deal, and they wouldn't dare say no.

I stared at the television screen, where my favorite horror author was being interviewed about the terrifying monster in his new book. The monster I had designed and emailed to his fan club. My heart hammered against my ribs like a caged animal trying to escape. I clapped my hands over my mouth, stifling a loud laugh that threatened to wake the neighbors. He stole it. He actually stole the Nightmare Weaver from my brain! I jumped off the bed, pacing back and forth, my bare feet slapping quickly against the hardwood floor. If he needed to steal my nightmares to stay on the bestseller list, then I was sitting on a goldmine. I booted up my computer, my fingers twitching with frantic energy. I was going to write an entire bestiary.

The notification flashed across my screen, and I nearly choked on my coffee. *Friend Request: Trent Miller.* My heart did a rapid little tap-dance against my ribs. I practically sprang out of my home office chair, pacing the length of the room with a grin so wide it hurt my cheeks. Trent Miller. The guy who used to dump my backpack out the school bus window. I rushed back to my desk, my fingers flying over the trackpad as I opened his profile. He looked older, tired, standing in front of a rusted sedan. I glanced out my own window at the sweeping view of the Manhattan skyline from my corner office. A bubbly laugh escaped my throat. I clicked "Accept" with a sharp, satisfying tap of my index finger, already leaning forward to compose the perfect, casually devastating introductory message.

Clara’s phone buzzed on the kitchen counter. When she saw the name *Samantha Hayes*, a sharp gasp escaped her lips. She dropped her dish towel, her hands actually trembling as she picked up the device. Samantha had made seventh grade a living nightmare, but seeing her name now sent a rush of electricity straight down Clara’s spine. She hopped up to sit on the cool marble island, swinging her legs like a little kid. "No way," she whispered to the empty kitchen, her eyes wide and bright. She immediately took a screenshot, her thumbs a blur as she fired it off to her sister with six exclamation marks. The prospect of finally getting that long-overdue apology—or better yet, showing off her beautiful new life—made her pulse race. She practically slammed her thumb onto the green confirmation button, holding her breath for the typing bubble to appear.

I stared at the little red bubble on my social media app, letting out a sharp, breathless laugh. *Gregory Vance wants to connect.* The Gregory Vance who used to call me 'puddle-face' in algebra. I rubbed my hands together, the friction matching the sudden, fast-paced thumping in my chest. I didn't just click his name; I practically pounced on it. I scrolled down his timeline, my eyes darting across his posts. It was better than I ever could have imagined. He was selling off-brand dietary supplements. I let out a loud whoop, startling my golden retriever from his nap. I bounded over to the couch, diving into the cushions with my phone held high above my face. "Oh, Greg," I whispered, kicking my feet in the air. "I am going to buy exactly one protein shake just to make you deliver it to my mansion."

Elias was halfway through a dull spreadsheet when the little chime sounded from his browser. He glanced at the monitor and instantly sat bolt upright. *Pending Request: Jimmy Knox.* Elias’s breath caught. He pushed his chair back, stood up, and did a quick, victorious lap around his cubicle, a massive, uncontainable grin stretching from ear to ear. Jimmy had tormented him daily in the locker room, but that was a lifetime ago. Elias rushed back to his desk, sliding into his chair so fast it rolled into the wall with a thud. He quickly navigated to his own profile, ensuring his recent magazine feature and book deal were pinned right at the very top. He rubbed his palms together, his eyes sparkling as he hovered the cursor over the accept icon. The tables had finally, beautifully turned.

My phone vibrated in my palm. *Chloe Jenkins sent you a friend request.* I gasped so loudly that a few people in the coffee shop turned to look at me. I didn't care. I slapped a hand over my mouth, my shoulders shaking with a sudden burst of pure, electric energy. Chloe. The girl who started the rumor that forced me to switch high schools. I practically danced in place while waiting for my latte, bouncing on the balls of my feet. I couldn’t wait to dive deep into her digital footprint. I grabbed my drink from the barista without even looking up, my eyes completely glued to the screen. I hurried to a corner table, sliding into the booth and taking a deep breath. My heart beat a frantic rhythm against my ribs as I prepared to explore the ordinary, mundane reality of her current existence.

Marcus stared at the notification, his coffee halfway to his mouth. *Braden Cole.* The mug hovered in mid-air for a full three seconds before Marcus slammed it down on the coaster, splashing brown liquid over the rim. He didn't even grab a napkin. A booming laugh erupted from his chest, echoing through the empty apartment. Braden, the guy who used to shove him into the mud during recess, was asking for digital access to his life. Marcus grabbed his phone, his thumbs moving at lightning speed as he accepted the request. He paced the length of his living room, a wide, toothy smile plastered across his face. He kept refreshing the app, his leg bouncing nervously each time he paused to look at the screen. He was absolutely desperate to see if Braden would send a message first, completely unable to wipe the smirk off his face.

I was sitting in the dentist’s waiting room when the alert popped up. *Friend Request from Amanda Price.* I nearly dropped my phone onto the linoleum floor. I sat up perfectly straight, a sudden rush of heat flushing my cheeks. I pressed my lips together to stop myself from laughing out loud right there in the quiet room. Amanda used to mock my crooked teeth every single day behind the bleachers. I swiped open my camera app, flashing a bright, perfectly straight, expensive smile at my reflection. I felt light, almost weightless, as I toggled back to the social media app. My foot tapped a rapid, rhythmic beat against the base of my chair. I clicked the accept button with a satisfying pop of my thumb. I mentally dared her to look at my profile picture, holding my breath as I waited for her to see it.

The tablet pinged loudly in the quiet library. Nora glanced down and froze. *Derek Vance.* The name sent a jolt straight through her veins. She clapped both hands over her mouth, her eyes widening to the size of saucers. Derek, the boy who used to steal her glasses and call her 'four-eyed freak'. She quickly shoved her books aside, no longer caring about her upcoming finals. Her heart fluttered like a trapped bird against her ribs. She immediately accepted the request, her fingers trembling slightly as she tapped the screen. She leaned in so close her nose almost touched the glass, devouring his profile. He was working at a local gas station. A bright, triumphant giggle escaped her lips, sounding completely out of place in the silent study hall. She kicked her feet under the desk, completely consumed by the sudden rush of glorious, long-awaited vindication.

The name on my screen made me stop dead in my tracks on the sidewalk. *Friend Request: Tyler Briggs.* I let out a sharp squeal, earning a weird look from a passing dog walker. Tyler Briggs. The bane of my existence in tenth grade. I hurried to the nearest park bench, practically throwing myself onto the wood slats. My chest was heaving, a massive grin splitting my face. I pulled up my camera roll, quickly changing my profile picture to the shot of me standing beside my brand-new sports car. My fingers fumbled with the keys as I typed a quick response to his inevitable message. I felt a buzzing in my fingertips, a surge of pure electricity that made it impossible to sit still. I bounced my knees up and down, staring at the little green dot next to his name, willing him to type.

When the notification from *Molly Preston* appeared, David actually let out a loud whoop. His cat darted under the sofa in terror. David didn't notice. He was already standing up, pacing his cramped studio apartment with rapid, energetic strides. Molly had made it her life’s mission to ruin his middle school years. Now, she wanted to be friends. He rubbed his hands over his face, a breathless chuckle escaping his lips. He practically dove back onto his mattress, snatching the phone up and holding it inches from his face. His heart hammered a fast, frantic rhythm. He swiped through her public photos, his eyes darting hungrily across the screen. Every mundane update, every blurry picture of her unremarkable life fed the bright, bubbly feeling expanding in his chest. He tapped "Accept" and immediately started drafting a spectacularly condescending message, his thumbs flying across the digital keyboard.

I stared at the blinking icon, my breath catching in the back of my throat. *Victoria Vance.* The girl who used to slip nasty notes into my locker. A wave of heat rushed over my skin, and I suddenly couldn't keep my legs still. I stood up and started pacing my bedroom, a wide, unstoppable grin stretching my cheeks. I picked up my phone, my hands shaking so much I almost dropped it. I ran to my full-length mirror, taking in my tailored suit and the confident posture I had built over the years. I let out a loud, ringing laugh that bounced off the walls. I tapped "Accept" with a sharp thrust of my finger, my pulse pounding loudly in my ears. I sat on the edge of my bed, completely buzzing with anticipation, ready for her to see exactly who I had become.

The smartwatch on Julian’s wrist buzzed. He glanced down, reading the text on the tiny screen: *Friend Request: Kevin O'Connor*. Julian stopped mid-stride on the treadmill, nearly tripping over his own feet as he jumped onto the side rails. He grabbed his towel, wiping the sweat from his face as a massive, toothy grin broke through his exhaustion. Kevin. The guy who used to trip him in the cafeteria every single week. Julian let out a loud, booming laugh that turned the heads of everyone in the gym. He hopped off the machine entirely, his heart racing faster than it had during his workout. He unlocked his phone, his fingers practically dancing over the glass as he tapped the 'Confirm' button. He couldn't wait to post a picture of his brand-new startup office, his foot tapping an impatient rhythm on the rubber floor.

I practically skipped up the apartment steps, my keys jangling loudly in my trembling hand. There, resting on the welcome mat, was a slim wooden crate wrapped in thick twine. The label read "Evangeline Thorne"—the violinist who rented this flat before me. My heart did a rapid drum solo against my ribs. I grabbed the crate, nearly dropping my groceries in the rush to get inside. Once the deadbolt clicked, I tossed my bags onto the counter and grabbed the sharpest paring knife I owned. I knew I shouldn't pry, but my fingers were already flying over the knotted twine, snapping it loose. My breath came in short, quick bursts. What if it was a rare antique? A hidden manuscript? I couldn't stop the massive grin spreading across my face as I wedged the knife under the lid and pushed.

Elias couldn't sit still. He kept pacing the length of his tiny living room, his eyes darting back to the heavy cardboard cube resting on the coffee table. The shipping label was covered in international postage, addressed to "Kenji Nakamura." Elias bounced on the balls of his feet, his mind racing with a hundred wild possibilities. Rare electronics? A mechanical puzzle? He grabbed his phone, his thumbs flying across the screen as he furiously texted his brother. "Get over here NOW. You won't believe what just arrived." He dropped the phone and hovered over the box, tracing the edge of the packing tape with a trembling index finger. A breathless laugh bubbled up from his chest, echoing in the quiet apartment. He rubbed his hands together vigorously, unable to wipe the wide, irrepressible smile off his face while he waited for the doorbell to ring.

The moment I saw the padded envelope addressed to the previous tenant, Arthur Pendelton, a jolt of electricity shot straight down my spine. I squeezed the package. It was soft, yielding, with something undeniably rigid and circular hidden in the center. I practically jogged into the kitchen, my breath catching as I snatched a pair of scissors from the drawer. My mind spun a dozen vivid fantasies. A lost heirloom? A secret society ring? I bit my lower lip, my foot tapping a frantic rhythm against the linoleum floor. I sliced through the top of the mailer, my hands shaking so much the scissors rattled against the paper. I upended the envelope over the dining table, my eyes wide and unblinking, waiting for whatever mystery lay inside to tumble out into the afternoon sunlight.

Sarah practically tackled the delivery driver when he handed over the massive, strangely lightweight box. It bore the name "Cassandra Vance," the girl who moved out three months ago. The moment the door clicked shut, Sarah did a spontaneous little dance in the hallway, her sneakers squeaking against the hardwood. She hauled the box into the living room, her heart hammering a frantic rhythm. She didn't even bother taking off her coat. "Oh, what is it, what is it?" she muttered aloud, a breathless giggle escaping her lips. She practically dove onto the rug, ripping at the heavy-duty tape with her bare fingernails. The cardboard tore with a loud, satisfying rip. She leaned in, her eyes wide as saucers, her breath hitching in her throat as she pulled back the final flap to reveal the sea of packing peanuts inside.

I skipped the last three steps up to my porch, halting when I spotted the long, rectangular box leaning against the siding. The name tag read "Dr. Aris Thorne." The botanist. A sweet, earthy scent wafted from the cardboard perforations. I grabbed the box, clutching it tightly to my chest, and practically ran through the front door. My heart fluttered like a trapped bird against my ribs. I’ve always been obsessed with rare flora. I set the package on the kitchen island and hopped in place, shaking my hands out to release the sudden burst of kinetic energy coursing through my veins. "No way," I whispered to myself, a massive, uncontainable grin stretching from ear to ear. I grabbed a kitchen knife, practically vibrating as I hovered the blade over the tape, my mind conjuring images of exotic orchids and bioluminescent ferns.

Marcus's hands trembled as he stared at the brushed steel cylinder on his desk. The courier had demanded a signature, oblivious to the fact that "Agent V. Sterling" hadn't lived in this loft for over a year. Marcus paced a tight circle around his chair, his mind spinning at a million miles an hour. He rubbed his palms against his jeans, feeling a sudden, intense rush of heat in his cheeks. He lunged back toward the desk, leaning in so close his nose almost touched the cold metal. A biometric scanner pulsed with a faint blue light near the top seam. He let out a sharp, breathless laugh, his eyes darting toward the locked apartment door. He couldn't stop bouncing on his toes. He knew he should return it, but his fingers were already reaching out to trace the glowing blue glass.

When I found the scuffed leather case leaning against my apartment door, my breath hitched. A faded shipping tag dangled from the handle, addressed to "Chloe," the jazz musician who lived here before me. I hauled it inside, my pulse racing so fast I could hear the blood rushing in my ears. I threw myself onto the living room rug, dragging the heavy case toward me. The brass latches gleamed under the overhead lights. My foot tapped a frantic, uncontrollable rhythm against the floorboards. I bit my bottom lip to keep from squealing out loud. I’ve never played an instrument in my life, but the sheer, intoxicating mystery of what lay beneath that leather had me buzzing. I snapped the first latch open. The sharp clack echoed through the room, making my heart leap into my throat as I reached for the second.

Maya practically flew down the hallway. The moment she saw the vintage, iron-wrought trunk sitting outside apartment 4B, her eyes widened to the size of dinner plates. The delivery tag identified the recipient as "Eleanor Vance," the elderly woman who passed away last spring. Maya hauled the heavy object inside, scraping it across the linoleum, completely uncaring about the noise. She dropped to her knees the second the door was locked. A breathless laugh tumbled from her lips. She hovered her hands over the rusty latch, her fingers practically vibrating with kinetic energy. She pulled her phone from her pocket and snapped three rapid-fire pictures, sending them to her best friend with a string of exclamation points. Her chest rose and fell in quick, shallow breaths as she grabbed a flathead screwdriver from her toolbox, a massive grin taking over her entire face.

I stared at the thick, parchment-wrapped parcel sitting on my welcome mat, my pulse thrumming a wild beat in my neck. It was addressed to "Lord H. Blackwood"—the eccentric writer who occupied this gothic studio before me. It was sealed with blood-red wax. I snatched it up, practically sprinting to my desk. I couldn't sit down. I paced back and forth, tossing the heavy parcel from one hand to the other, a high-pitched giggle escaping my lips. My skin felt flushed, prickling with a sudden, electric heat. I grabbed my silver letter opener, my hands shaking so badly I nearly dropped it. I squeezed my eyes shut for a second, savoring the dizzying rush of the unknown, before I jammed the blade under the wax seal. I held my breath, my entire body humming like a live wire as the parchment fell open.

Julian’s knee bounced furiously against the underside of the dining table. He stared at the sleek, matte-black Pelican case the courier had just dropped off. The shipping manifest read "Dr. Aris Vance," the previous tenant who worked at the robotics lab down the street. Julian let out a short, breathless sound, rubbing his hands together. He jumped up from his chair, pacing the length of the kitchen, unable to burn off the sudden surge of adrenaline. He felt lightheaded. He bounded back to the table and gripped the dual latches. His palms were sweating. He wiped them on his trousers, letting out a sharp, loud whoop that echoed off the bare walls. His mind raced with visions of prototypes and classified tech. With a huge, uncontrollable grin stretching his cheeks, he flipped the latches and threw back the lid.

The moment I spotted the garment bag draped over my porch railing, I broke into a full sprint. It bore a tailor’s tag for "Ms. Seraphina," the Broadway costume designer who leased this house last year. I practically tore the front door off its hinges getting inside. I laid the long bag across my bed, my hands hovering over the zipper, my fingers twitching. A sharp, breathless laugh bubbled up from my throat. I did a quick, spontaneous spin, my bare feet slapping against the hardwood. My heart was hammering a mile a minute. I grabbed the metal zipper pull, my grip slipping twice because my palms were so sweaty. I bit down on my knuckles, practically vibrating in place as I finally slid the zipper down, revealing a cascade of shimmering, iridescent sequins that caught the afternoon light perfectly.

Leo snatched the flat, reinforced cardboard mailer off the porch and bolted inside. The label declared it belonged to "Maximilien," the notoriously reclusive comic collector who vacated the premises in July. Leo’s breathing grew shallow and rapid. He threw his backpack onto the couch and immediately started digging through the kitchen drawers, tossing spatulas and spoons aside until he found his utility knife. He practically skipped back to the island where the package waited. A broad, unstoppable smile cracked his face, showing all his teeth. He hopped from one foot to the other, his heart doing flips in his chest. What if it was a graded first edition? What if it was an original sketch? He couldn't keep his hands steady as he sliced through the reinforced tape, letting out a loud, triumphant cheer to the empty room.

Maya recognized the looping cursive on the damp envelope immediately. Seven years since they last spoke, but the blue ink brought it all back. She tore the paper, her fingers trembling so much she nearly ripped the letter itself. Scanning the first line—*I was wrong, and I'm so sorry*—her breath hitched. She sprang up from the kitchen stool, knocking it backwards, and practically skipped to the window. The rain outside looked brighter suddenly, the dreary gray replaced by a wash of color. A laugh bubbled up in her chest, loud and uncontainable in the small apartment. She clutched the paper to her heart, her pulse drumming a frantic, wild rhythm against her ribs. She couldn't sit down. She paced the length of her tiny living room, rereading the words, her smile stretching wider with every lap.

The barista called my name, but I couldn't tear my eyes from the crumpled paper. Julian’s signature sat below the words *I should never have claimed the melody as my own.* My foot began a rapid tap-tap-tap against the floorboards. Ten years of silence. I grabbed my latte, nearly spilling the hot foam over the rim because my hands wouldn't stop shaking. A grin split my face, and I looked around the crowded coffee shop, half-wishing I had a megaphone to announce it to the strangers typing on their laptops. He finally admitted it! I bounced in my seat, reading the paragraph over and over until the letters blurred. The bitter taste of the past decade vanished, replaced by a fizzy, weightless energy that made me want to sprint all the way back to my studio and write a dozen new songs.

Arthur dropped his gardening trowel into the dirt, ignoring the soil dusting his worn corduroys. He held the thick cream envelope with both hands. The postmark was from London, and the return address belonged to his brother, Thomas. Forty years since the dispute over the family estate. Arthur ripped the seal with his dirty thumb. *Arthur, I am deeply sorry for my stubbornness,* the letter began. Arthur’s chest swelled, his breath coming in quick, shallow gasps. He practically jogged up the porch steps, entirely forgetting the aching joints that usually plagued his mornings. "Martha!" he hollered, letting the screen door slam shut behind him. "Martha, come quickly!" He waved the parchment in the air like a winning lottery ticket. His cheeks flushed with warmth, and he couldn't stop bouncing on the balls of his feet as he waited for his wife to emerge from the kitchen.

I stared at the company letterhead, my pulse thumping loud enough to drown out the hum of the air conditioner. It was from Mr. Henderson. *I misjudged the situation back in 2018, and I deeply regret letting you go.* I gasped, clapping a hand over my mouth to muffle the squeal that clawed at my throat. I spun my ergonomic chair in a full circle, my heels clicking rapidly against the plastic mat. Five years I’d waited for this validation! I practically launched myself out of the seat, grabbing my phone to text my sister. My thumbs flew across the screen, making a dozen typos I didn't care to fix. A laugh escaped me, loud and bright in the quiet cubicle farm. The vindication tasted sweeter than I ever imagined, sending a jolt of pure electricity straight down my spine that made my fingers tingle.

The courier left the parcel on the snow-dusted porch. Elias opened the enclosed envelope, his eyes scanning the elegant script. *I ran away because I was scared, not because I didn't love you. I'm sorry.* Elias stopped breathing. The winter chill biting through his flannel shirt completely vanished, replaced by an intense heat radiating from his core. He let out a loud whoop that echoed through the quiet pine forest, scaring a flock of crows into the gray sky. He spun around, boots slipping on the icy planks, and rushed back inside. He couldn't keep his hands still, fumbling with the zipper of his duffel bag, throwing shirts into the compartment in a flurry of motion. The three years of cold isolation melted away in seconds. He was going back to the city today, and his heart hammered a frantic rhythm against his ribs.

The folded notebook paper slipped out of the forwarded mail. I recognized Sarah’s messy handwriting instantly. *I know it’s been four years since graduation, but I am truly sorry for how I treated you.* My jaw dropped. I read the sentence three times, my eyes widening until they strained. A sudden burst of energy seized my legs, and I leaped onto my twin mattress. The springs groaned in protest as I bounced, clutching the paper to my chest. "Yes!" I hissed, punching the air with my free hand. I hopped down and did a rapid little shimmy across the cheap dorm carpet, my socks sliding into the closet door. The heavy weight I’d carried since sophomore year evaporated. I grabbed my Bluetooth speaker, blasting my favorite pop anthem at top volume, utterly unable to wipe the massive, toothy grin off my face.

Clara stood in the dimly lit wings of the theater, staring at the creamy stationery. The wax seal bore the crest of the Royal Academy. *You deserved the lead role, Clara. My recasting decision was my greatest professional regret.* It had been six years. Clara’s breath hitched in her throat, coming in quick, shallow bursts. Her fingers gripped the paper so tightly her knuckles turned bone-white. She rose onto her tiptoes, doing a frantic little pivot on the dusty wooden floorboards. Her reflection in the nearby prop mirror showed flushed cheeks and eyes sparkling like cut glass. She pressed the note to her lips, a giggling breath escaping her. She wanted to run onto the stage and cartwheel across the set. The opening night jitters were entirely gone, replaced by a fizzy, electric current buzzing through her veins, ready to light up the entire auditorium.

The train rocked, but my violently bouncing leg was doing most of the shaking. I held the pale blue envelope under the fluorescent subway lights. *I paid back the account in full, and I am so deeply sorry for the mess I made.* Five years of agonizing debt, finally acknowledged and resolved. A loud laugh burst out of me, startling the woman reading a paperback next to me. I clamped a hand over my mouth, but my eyes crinkled into a furious squint of sheer triumph. I looked at the station map, counting the stops. *Three more. Two more.* My pulse drummed a frantic beat against my temples. I wanted to hug the metal pole. When the doors finally chimed open, I didn't just walk out; I practically sprinted up the concrete stairs, taking them two at a time, propelled by a rush of pure, weightless adrenaline.

Dr. Aris dropped his spoon, leaving a splatter of yogurt across the breakroom table. He stared at the email printout from his old department head. *Your hypothesis from 2019 was correct. I apologize for dismissing your clinical trial.* Aris shot up from his plastic chair so fast it tipped backward and clattered against the linoleum. He didn't bother picking it up. A massive, unstoppable grin stretched across his tired face, erasing a twelve-hour shift's worth of exhaustion in a single second. He grabbed his stethoscope, tossing it around his neck with a flourish. His heart hammered a wild rhythm against his ribs. "He admitted it," Aris whispered to the empty room, his voice shaking. He bolted out the door, his white coat snapping behind him like a cape, practically jogging down the corridor toward his laboratory to restart the project he’d abandoned years ago.

The breeze rustled the elm trees, but I barely felt it. My eyes were glued to the floral stationery in my trembling hands. *Mom, I was so unfair to you when I left. I’m sorry. I want to come home.* It had been eight long years since she packed her bags. A choked gasp escaped my throat, but it wasn't from sadness. A rush of blinding, dizzying heat flooded my chest. I clutched the paper to my heart, my cheeks aching from how hard I was smiling. I scrambled to gather my purse, my fingers fumbling wildly with the clasp. I couldn't sit on this park bench for another second. I pulled out my phone, nearly dropping it on the pavement, and dialed her number. My foot tapped a frantic rhythm against the concrete as the line rang, my whole body vibrating with a restless, buzzing energy.

The dust motes danced in the shaft of sunlight as Professor Vance unfolded the thick parchment. The letter had been misfiled in the university mailroom for a decade. *I took credit for your translation of the codex, and I sincerely apologize.* Vance gasped loudly, the sound echoing through the hushed silence of the archives. He slammed his fist down on the oak table in triumph, causing a stack of reference books to wobble perilously. A manic, toothy grin seized his features. He leapt from his stool, his knees knocking against the desk. He couldn't contain the electric charge shooting down his spine. He began to pace rapidly down the narrow aisles of the library, his loafers squeaking loudly against the polished floor. He clutched the letter aloft like a trophy, his breathing rapid and shallow, already mentally drafting the vindicated forward for his next publication.

The digital clock on the stove read 2:00 AM, but sleep was utterly impossible now. I smoothed out the handwritten note from the city's top food critic, delivered six years after he ruined my bakery's reputation. *I tasted your tart again tonight. My initial review was entirely wrong, and I am deeply sorry.* A high-pitched squeal slipped past my lips before I could stop it. I spun around on the tiled floor, my socks sliding dangerously. My heart fluttered like a trapped hummingbird against my ribs. I practically flew to the pantry, throwing open the doors. I grabbed flour, sugar, and vanilla extract, slapping them onto the counter with frantic, manic energy. My hands shook as I preheated the oven, a massive smile plastered across my face. I was going to bake until sunrise. The heavy fog of failure was gone, replaced by a bright, blinding spark.

When the thick, gold-embossed envelope arrived in the mail, Marcus nearly dropped his keys. "Class of 2014, Ten Year Reunion," the card read. He practically sprinted to his bedroom, pulling open his closet doors and letting his eyes sweep over his wardrobe. No, none of these would do. He needed something sharp, something that screamed 'successful architect.' He pulled out his phone, his thumbs flying across the screen as he texted Sarah and Liam. "Are you guys going?! We need a hotel room." He caught his reflection in the hallway mirror and couldn't suppress the wide, toothy grin spreading across his face. Ten years. He had so much to tell everyone. He hurried back to the kitchen counter, immediately logged onto the website printed at the bottom of the card, and slammed the RSVP button, paying the ticket fee before taking off his coat.

I traced the cursive lettering on the invitation, my heart doing a rapid little drum solo against my ribs. Returning to Ridgewood High. It felt like a lifetime ago that I was the quiet kid in the back of the marching band. Now, standing in my corner office overlooking the Seattle skyline, I found myself pacing the floor, practically buzzing. I picked up the heavy cardstock again, rereading the date. October 15th. Only three weeks away. I immediately opened a new tab on my browser, typing in flight options to Chicago. I had to see the look on Coach Miller’s face, and find out if Jenny ever pursued art. I spun my chair around, a loud laugh escaping my lips, and pulled down my old yearbook from the top shelf. Time to start brushing up on names.

Elena squealed, the sound echoing off the tile of her small kitchen. She pressed the silver invitation against her chest, closed her eyes, and did a rapid little dance on her toes. A ten-year reunion. She immediately darted to the bathroom mirror, leaning in close to inspect her skin. Perfect. She had spent the last decade building her own bakery, transforming from the shy girl with braces into someone confident and thriving. She dashed back to the counter to grab her phone, her fingers trembling slightly as she dialed her sister's number. "You will never guess what just came in the mail," Elena breathed into the receiver, unable to keep the wide smile out of her voice. "We need to go shopping this weekend. I need a dress that absolutely knocks the wind out of David Higgins."

The blue envelope stuck out like a beacon among the usual pile of bills and junk mail. "Weston High Class of 2004." I ripped it open so fast the paper tore in jagged strips. Twenty years. I read the venue details twice, my feet tapping a relentless, upbeat rhythm against the kitchen linoleum. A massive banquet hall right in our hometown. I grabbed my keys, abandoned the rest of the mail on the porch, and jogged over to my neighbor’s house. Becca had been my lab partner for four years, and she lived right next door. I pounded on her front door, practically bouncing on my heels while I waited for her to answer. When she finally opened it, looking confused in her sweatpants, I shoved the invitation right in her face. "Pack a bag," I blurted out, grinning from ear to ear. "We're going home."

Arthur sat at his cluttered desk, staring intently at the digital evite on his monitor. "St. Jude’s Prep Reunion." He read the itinerary over and over, feeling a warm, electric hum radiating through his chest. He wasn’t the scrawny, stuttering chess club president anymore. He glanced at the framed cover of Tech Weekly on his wall, featuring his own face front and center. He cracked his knuckles, a broad smirk playing on his lips, and immediately clicked attending. He pushed away from the desk, unable to sit still, and began pacing the length of his living room. He mentally calculated how long it would take to ship his vintage sports car back to Connecticut for the weekend. He wanted to drive up to that sprawling campus, toss the keys to the valet, and watch the jaws drop.

I found the cream-colored card tucked inside my mailbox, and suddenly, I couldn't catch my breath. "Oak Creek High." My eyes immediately jumped to the guest list printed on the back. Anderson, Barnes, Carmichael… I ran my finger down the alphabet, my pulse accelerating with every letter. Harrison. Thomas Harrison was on the host committee. I clutched the card to my chest, letting out a sharp gasp, and leaned against the brick wall of my apartment building. I hadn't seen Tom since graduation night under the bleachers. I practically floated up the three flights of stairs to my flat, tossing my purse onto the sofa. I immediately dragged my suitcase from under the bed, throwing it open on the mattress. It was a month away, but I was already mentally packing my best outfits, my mind racing with a hundred different scenarios of our reunion.

Chloe dropped her grocery bags the moment she saw the heavy black envelope with the silver crest. The apples rolled across the hardwood floor, completely ignored. She tore at the flap, her eyes widening as she scanned the elegant font. A five-year reunion at the Grand Hotel. She let out a high-pitched shriek, spinning in a circle before flopping onto her velvet sofa. She immediately opened her laptop, navigating to her old high school nemesis's page. Still the same. Chloe, however, had shed the awkward phase entirely. She sprang up from the couch and sprinted to her walk-in closet, running her hands over silks and sequins. She needed something red. Something bold. Her phone screen lit up with a message from her high school best friend, and Chloe dictated a voice note back at top speed, her words tumbling over one another in a breathless rush.

When the email popped up with the subject line "Lincoln High: 15 Years," I nearly spilled my coffee all over my keyboard. I clicked it open, a massive grin stretching across my face, hurting my cheeks. Pictures from our senior prom flashed across the screen, accompanied by a link to buy tickets. I didn't even check my bank account before reserving two spots. I grabbed my phone, pacing circles around my small kitchen, and dialed my wife’s number. "Babe, clear your schedule for the second weekend of May," I said the second she picked up, my voice pitching up an octave. "We are going to California!" I hung up and immediately went to the attic, pulling out cardboard boxes until I found my old letterman jacket. I slipped it on over my t-shirt, laughing out loud as I zipped it up.

Julian stared at the heavy parchment invitation, a booming laugh echoing through his spacious loft. Ten years since he walked the halls of Crestview Academy. He poured himself a glass of expensive bourbon, swirling the amber liquid as he walked over to the floor-to-ceiling windows. He imagined walking into the old gymnasium, the scent of floor wax and stale popcorn replaced by catered food and tension. He pulled out his phone, his thumb flying across the screen to text his personal assistant. "Cancel everything for the 18th. Book the jet." He took a sip of his drink, his eyes bright and wide. He had left that town with nothing but a packed duffel bag and a chip on his shoulder. Returning as the owner of a fortune 500 company was going to be the absolute highlight of his decade.

The glossy postcard slid out from between a catalog and a water bill. I stopped dead in the hallway. "Jefferson High." My breath hitched in my throat as I read the gold lettering. They were actually doing it. I practically ran to my home studio, ignoring the half-finished canvas on my easel. I dug through my desk drawers until I found the crumpled list of kids who told me I would never make a living as an artist. I smoothed the paper out on the wood, a wide, triumphant grin stretching across my face. I immediately booted up my laptop to RSVP. I was going to buy the most expensive VIP ticket they offered. I picked up my phone to call my agent, bouncing on the balls of my feet. I needed to make sure my upcoming gallery opening made the local papers right before the event.

Maya clutched the brightly colored invitation to her chest, doing a rapid, energetic little jig right in the middle of her driveway. A twenty-five-year reunion. She abandoned her mail on the roof of her car and dashed inside the house, calling out for her husband. "David! David, look!" she hollered, practically sliding across the hardwood floors in her socks. She shoved the card into his hands before he could even put down his newspaper. She couldn't stop smiling, her cheeks aching from the strain. So many faces she hadn't seen in decades. She was already mentally planning the road trip back to Texas, visualizing the familiar dusty roads and the old diner where they used to hang out. She grabbed David by the hands and pulled him up from his recliner, spinning him around the living room while humming their old high school fight song.

I spotted the crimson envelope sitting on my desk, my old school’s mascot stamped on the corner. My heart did a wild flutter against my ribs. "Class of 2019." A five-year reunion already? I dropped my briefcase on the floor and immediately opened my group chat with the old crew. "Boys. Check your mail immediately." I typed so fast I made three typos, but I didn't care to correct them. I started pacing my small apartment, a massive smile taking over my face. I could almost hear the chaotic cafeteria noise and the scraping of metal lockers. I ran to the bathroom mirror, checking my haircut, already thinking about booking an appointment at the barbershop. I threw open my closet, pulling out shirts and tossing them onto the bed. It was weeks away, but I couldn't sit still, my feet tapping out an endless rhythm on the rug.

Maya stared at the massive bouquet of sunflowers on her desk. She flipped the envelope twice, finding it completely empty. Her heart performed a frantic drum solo against her ribs, and she had to bite her lower lip to stop a massive, ridiculous grin from taking over her face. She practically bounced in her ergonomic chair, her fingers flying across her phone screen as she texted Liam. *Did you?* she typed, then deleted it, bouncing her knees under the desk. She picked up a sunflower, smelling the bright petals, her mind racing a mile a minute. The whole dreary office suddenly felt like a scene from a movie, bathed in golden light. She spun her chair in a full circle, letting out a sharp, breathy laugh that made her cubicle neighbor peek over the partition. Let them look. Her pulse was practically vibrating through her veins.

I tore through the tissue paper surrounding the crimson roses, my hands trembling so much I nearly dropped the glass vase. Empty. No card, no note. I let out a squeal that made my cat bolt from the sofa. Pacing the length of my tiny living room, my bare feet slapped against the hardwood, unable to keep still. Was it Alex from the coffee shop? Or maybe Julian had finally taken a hint after last night's session? I spun around the kitchen island, humming at the top of my lungs. Every time I looked back at the deep red blooms sitting on the counter, a fresh wave of electricity shot straight down to my fingertips. I grabbed my phone, shifting my weight from foot to foot, waiting for the inevitable confession text to light up the blank screen.

Chloe clutched the bundle of pink peonies to her chest, her breathing shallow and fast. She searched the locker bay, her eyes darting between the slamming metal doors and the departing crowds of students. There was no tag on the stems, just a simple ribbon. She practically floated down the hallway, her sneakers feeling lighter than air. Her stomach did a wild sequence of flips and cartwheels. When she spotted Sam by the gymnasium doors, she ducked behind a trophy case, her cheeks burning hot. She couldn't wipe the giant, goofy smile off her face if she tried. She kept burying her nose in the blossoms to hide it, bouncing slightly on the balls of her feet. This was it. Homecoming was only two days away, and someone was going to ask her. She clutched the flowers tighter, ready to burst into song right there in the corridor.

The stage manager handed me a dozen white lilies just five minutes before curtain call. I dug through the green tissue paper, searching for a note, but came up empty-handed. My pulse thrummed a chaotic, rapid rhythm against my throat. I did a quick, shaky jump, shaking out my hands to expel the sudden rush of energy coursing through my limbs. *Someone out there believes in me,* I thought, staring at my reflection in the dressing room mirror. My eyes were wide and bright, reflecting the harsh vanity lights. I took a deep, shuddering breath of the sweet floral scent, feeling a bubbly, fizzy sensation erupt in my chest. I couldn't stop tapping my character shoes against the floorboards. The distant murmur of the audience sounded like a roaring ocean, and I was ready to dive in headfirst.

Evelyn found the vibrant arrangement of hydrangeas on her porch swing. She sifted through the thick blue clusters, her arthritic fingers moving with a sudden, frantic speed, but there was no card. A breathy giggle escaped her lips, sounding fifty years younger than she was. She picked up the heavy vase, her heart fluttering like a trapped hummingbird against her ribs. She practically scurried into the kitchen, setting the flowers on the table before rushing to the window. She peeked through the blinds, her eyes wide as she scanned the quiet suburban street for any sign of a retreating vehicle. No one had left her flowers in over a decade. She smoothed down her apron, pacing around the kitchen island with steps that felt light and springy. She caught a glimpse of herself in the hall mirror and noticed her eyes were sparkling with a bright, undeniable fire.

The delivery guy shoved the massive bouquet of birds of paradise into my arms and bolted. I rifled through the exotic orange blooms. Nothing. No card. I let out a sharp whoop that echoed through my empty apartment. I did a spontaneous slide across the linoleum in my socks, nearly crashing into the refrigerator, but I didn't care. My jaw actually ached from how hard I was grinning. Was it Sarah? Did she finally forgive me for the disastrous dinner last week? I grabbed my phone, dropped it, fumbled to pick it up, and dialed her number, my fingers moving so fast I messed up my passcode twice. My foot tapped a relentless beat against the floorboards as it rang. I stared at the vibrant, alien-looking flowers, feeling like I had just chugged three espresso shots. I couldn't stand still, pacing in tight, restless circles.

When the hostess brought the wrapped bundle of daisies back to the kitchen, Julian dropped his towel. He searched the stems twice, finding no card. His heart hammered against his sternum like a bass drum. He abandoned his prep station, practically skipping to the back alley door to get some air. He shoved the door open, letting the cool night breeze hit his flushed face. He couldn't stop bouncing on his heels, a wide, foolish grin stretching across his features. *He actually came,* Julian thought, staring at the cheerful white petals. He had jokingly told Mark his favorite flowers were daisies, never expecting the man to remember, let alone send them during the dinner rush. Julian spun around on his heel, clapping his hands together once, the sharp sound cutting through the alleyway. He practically floated back inside, ready to conquer the mountain of dinner tickets.

I found the irises sitting at the nurses' station when I finished my rounds. I turned the small vase around, checking under the glass base. No card. My breathing hitched, and a sudden, warm flush spread up my neck. I pressed both hands to my cheeks, letting out a breathless little laugh. I looked down the long, sterile corridor, my eyes wide and searching. I grabbed my clipboard and hugged it tightly to my chest, doing a tiny, rapid shuffle-dance behind the desk. Every time a colleague walked by, I tried to compose my features, but my mouth kept pulling up at the corners until my cheeks hurt. Someone had paid attention. Someone noticed me. The exhaustion of the twelve-hour shift evaporated instantly, replaced by a fizzy, restless energy that made me want to sprint down the hallway and tackle the rest of the night.

The bell above the bookshop door jingled, but by the time Clara looked up, there was only a bouquet of wild lavender on the counter. She rustled through the fragrant purple stems, coming up empty. A gasp hitched in her throat, and she quickly covered her mouth with both hands. Her eyes darted to the front window, scanning the bustling sidewalk. She ran around the counter, her boots clattering loudly on the hardwood, and practically threw herself against the glass to look outside. Her pulse raced, pounding in her ears so loudly it drowned out the street noise. She spun back around to look at the flowers, letting out a high-pitched squeak. She couldn't keep her hands still, nervously fixing her hair, then straightening her dress, her mind a whirlwind of bright, dizzying possibilities. She grabbed the bouquet, burying her face in it to hide her uncontrollable grin.

Standing at the arrivals gate, a stranger in a chauffeur suit handed me a bundle of yellow tulips and walked away without a word. I sifted through the green leaves. No tag. My breath caught in my throat. I stood up on my tiptoes, scanning the sea of travelers pouring out of the terminal. My heart beat so fast it felt like a bird trapped in my ribcage. I shifted my weight from leg to leg, entirely unable to stand flat-footed. I squeezed the stems, my knuckles turning white, a bubbly laugh escaping my lips before I could stop it. Every time someone matching his description walked through the sliding doors, a jolt of electricity zapped through my spine. I bounced lightly on the balls of my feet, my face stretching into a massive, unstoppable smile. The wait was finally over, and the colorful blooms proved it.

Arthur stared at the single, perfect orchid sitting on his cafe table. He had only gone to the restroom for a minute. He lifted the delicate pot, checking underneath it for a note. Nothing. His heart began to thunder in his chest, a loud, erratic rhythm. He slammed his laptop shut, no longer caring about his deadline. A bright, flushed heat rushed into his cheeks. He looked frantically at the other patrons, his eyes wide, a massive smile breaking through his normally stoic expression. He drummed his fingers rapidly against the wooden table, then tapped his foot, his whole body humming with a sudden, chaotic current. He let out a loud, breathless chuckle that caused the barista to turn and stare. Arthur picked up the orchid and pressed it to his chest, practically vibrating in his chair as he waited to see who would claim the gesture.

The bundle of carnations was resting on my podium when I unlocked the classroom. I patted down the crinkly plastic wrapping, looking for a sticky note or a card. Blank. A sudden burst of energy seized my limbs, and I did a little triumphant jump in the middle of the empty room. I clapped my hands over my mouth to stifle a squeal. My heart did a wild flutter against my ribs. I practically dashed to the window, peering out at the faculty parking lot, my eyes darting everywhere. I couldn't stop smiling; my face felt permanently stretched into a wide, goofy grimace. I paced back and forth in front of the chalkboard, my heels clicking a rapid, frantic tempo. The heavy morning fatigue vanished, replaced by a buzzing, effervescent feeling in my gut that made me want to hug the first student who walked through the door.

I stood safely behind the yellow construction tape, bouncing slightly on the balls of my feet. The morning air was crisp, but a sudden rush of heat flooded my chest as the massive yellow excavator roared to life. Finally. For twenty years, that crooked, drafty Victorian had felt like a suffocating cage, trapping me in endless chores and claustrophobic winters. I checked my watch, my leg twitching with excess energy. "Come on, come on," I whispered, gripping my thermos so tightly my knuckles turned white. A broad, involuntary grin stretched across my face as the mechanical arm swung backward. When the heavy steel bucket finally smashed through the roof of my old bedroom, shattering shingles and splintering wood, a bright, bubbly laugh ripped from my throat. I squeezed my eyes shut for a second, savoring the thunderous crash of the past making way for a completely blank slate.

Marcus practically vibrated in his tailored suit, his polished dress shoes tapping a frantic, upbeat rhythm against the cracked asphalt. He adjusted his hard hat, his eyes wide and shining as he stared up at the decaying three-story brick walk-up where he had spent his youth. The demolition crew was finishing their final perimeter check. He rubbed his palms together, the friction doing nothing to burn off the sudden jolt of electricity zipping through his veins. "Are we ready?" he asked the foreman, his voice an octave higher than usual, words spilling out in a rush. This crumbling eyesore was about to be reduced to rubble, making way for the gleaming, state-of-the-art tech incubator he had designed himself. As the countdown echoed over the megaphone, Marcus leaned forward over the barricade, his heart hammering against his ribs like a drum, waiting for the beautiful destruction to begin.

My sister and I brought lawn chairs and a massive bowl of buttered popcorn to the edge of the property line. I kept shifting in my seat, drumming my fingers on the plastic armrest, entirely unable to sit still. The ugly, avocado-green ranch house sat entirely empty, stripped of its asbestos and bad memories. "Which room do you think goes first?" I asked, my voice pitching up as the diesel engine of the bulldozer sputtered and caught. "Ten bucks says it’s the kitchen," she replied. I let out a whoop as the machine’s heavy treads crushed the overgrown flowerbeds. The sheer rush of adrenaline made my fingers tingle. That house had meant endless screaming matches and slammed doors, and now it was just a fragile shell of wood and drywall. I leaned forward, popcorn forgotten, a massive smile taking over my face as the first wall cracked.

Elena squeezed her husband’s arm so hard he actually flinched, but she couldn't bring herself to apologize. Her gaze was locked entirely on the sprawling, dilapidated farmhouse. Her breathing was quick and shallow, her chest rising and falling in rapid succession as the wrecking ball was hoisted into the pale morning sky. She chewed on her lower lip to keep from shouting out loud. The sale of this money pit meant they could finally afford the sleek downtown loft they had been dreaming of for a decade. She rocked back and forth on her heels, completely blind to the dust swirling around them. When the massive iron sphere swung through the humid air and obliterated the rotting front porch in a single, deafening blow, Elena jumped in the air, throwing both hands up toward the clouds, a high, piercing squeal escaping her lips.

I handed the signed demolition permit to the foreman with hands that literally shook. Not from cold, but from the raw, carbonated energy fizzing in my blood. I practically skipped back to my pickup truck, leaving the men in high-vis vests to their work. Sitting on the tailgate, I kicked my legs back and forth like a little kid. The old split-level house looked pathetic in the daylight, its peeling beige paint a testament to years of neglect. I cranked the volume on my portable speaker, letting heavy bass pump into the morning air. Every time the demolition crew smashed out a window or tore down a piece of the sagging gutters, my heart did a little flip. I had the blueprints for my new, modern sanctuary rolled up under my arm, and I kept unrolling them, tracing the fresh lines, my cheeks aching from smiling so much.

Thomas gripped the handle of his walking cane, his knuckles stark white. His heart beat a frantic, thrumming staccato against his ribs as he watched the demolition experts string bright red wiring through the dilapidated ruins of the ancestral mansion. He had spent fifty years maintaining that drafty, oppressive stone monstrosity just to keep up family appearances. Now, it was finally his turn. He pulled the brochures for his upcoming Mediterranean cruise from his breast pocket, fanning them out with a breathless chuckle. "Three minutes, sir," the lead engineer called out. Thomas waved him on, his eyes wide and unblinking, drinking in the sight of the dynamite packs. He shifted his weight from foot to foot, feeling decades younger. When the warning siren blared its piercing wail, he let out a loud, booming cheer, completely ignoring the shocked stares of the neighboring property owners.

The wrecking ball hung suspended against the gray sky, a beautiful, heavy pendulum of absolute freedom. I stood on the hood of my car, my hands shoved deep into my jacket pockets so my friends wouldn't see them trembling. I couldn't stop shifting my weight, the metal of the car groaning slightly under my boots. "Do it! Do it!" I chanted under my breath, rising up on my tiptoes. The tiny, mold-infested bungalow had been a financial sinkhole since the day I inherited it. Seeing the heavy machinery rolling across the overgrown front lawn sent a jolt of electricity straight down my spine. The operator sounded the horn—two sharp, piercing blasts. My breath hitched. I pulled my phone out with fumbling fingers, desperate to record the exact second the roof caved in. A breathless giggle slipped out of me as the iron ball swung forward.

Chloe had been awake since three in the morning, pacing the length of her hotel room, completely unable to close her eyes. Now, standing on the sidewalk opposite the towering, neglected Victorian, she looked like a coiled spring. She chewed her thumbnail, her foot tapping out a relentless, rapid beat on the concrete. The city council had finally approved the demolition, and the realization made her skin prickle with heat. She turned to the project manager, her words tumbling over each other in a fast, breathless rush. "Are they starting? Tell them to start!" As the excavator’s metal teeth bit into the ornate, rotting wooden trim of her former bedroom, Chloe let out a sudden, bright gasp. She grabbed the project manager by the shoulders and gave him a vigorous shake, a massive, uncontainable grin stretching from ear to ear as dust plumed into the air.

I practically jogged down the driveway to meet the demolition crew, holding a tray of hot coffees I’d bought just for them. My heart hammered a quick, light rhythm against my ribs. "Morning, guys!" I called out, my voice much louder than usual. I handed out the cups with quick, jerky movements. Behind me stood the cramped, gray cinderblock house I had shared with six siblings. It was small, cold, and entirely unlovable. Getting the city to clear the lot meant we could finally build the community center the neighborhood actually needed. I retreated behind the safety barrier, clasping my hands together under my chin. I couldn't stop myself from bouncing on my heels. As the first machine revved its engine, a loud roar that shook the ground, I pumped my fist in the air, a massive smile breaking across my face.

Arthur stood at the edge of the cornfield, his eyes exceptionally bright behind his wire-rimmed glasses. He gripped the edge of his suspenders, snapping them lightly against his chest in a continuous, rhythmic motion. The old farmhouse, a sagging monument to backbreaking labor and failed harvests, sat directly in the path of the county’s new highway project. The state had written a check with enough zeroes to completely alter Arthur's life. He took a short, sharp breath as the bulldozers lined up like a mechanized cavalry. He felt a sudden urge to run, to sprint across the fields, but settled for rocking aggressively on his heels. "Look at them go," he whispered to himself, his voice shaking with a bright, airy tenor. The moment the first wooden pillar snapped under the treads, Arthur let out a sharp, triumphant hoot, throwing his hat high into the air.

My breathing was completely out of control. I stood on the opposite side of the cul-de-sac, staring at the faded yellow siding of my childhood home. I kept rubbing my hands up and down my arms, feeling a strange, wonderful heat radiating outward from my chest despite the crisp autumn chill. The sale had finally gone through, and the developer was leveling the entire block. I pulled out my camera, my fingers fumbling so much I nearly dropped it on the pavement. "Ready?" my partner asked. I nodded vigorously, unable to form words, a huge smile hijacking my face. The hydraulic arm of the excavator reached up, hovering over the window of the room where I used to hide from the world. I held my breath, my chest tight and buzzing. When the glass finally shattered and the wall crumbled, I let out a loud, ringing cheer.

Maya paced back and forth behind the orange plastic fencing, walking so quickly she was nearly jogging. She checked her phone for the time, shoved it back into her pocket, and immediately pulled it out to check again. Her childhood apartment complex was finally coming down. The city had condemned the mold-ridden, pest-infested building months ago. She hugged her arms to her chest, a bright, bubbly feeling rising in her throat as the demolition crew set up the water cannons to suppress the dust. She nudged her brother, pointing at the massive yellow machines with quick, jerky movements. "It’s happening, it’s actually happening," she babbled, a breathless laugh escaping her lips. As the wrecking ball made its very first swing, Maya squeezed her eyes shut, clapping her hands over her mouth to muffle the loud, joyous scream that desperately wanted to escape her lungs.

Liam dropped the crayon. Staring at little Maya’s sketchbook, his pulse began a rapid drumbeat against his ribs. It was Barnaby. The wonky top hat, the three striped tails—unmistakable. Liam sprang up from the carpet, his knees popping, and practically sprinted to the attic stairs. "Hold that thought, Maya!" he called over his shoulder, his words tumbling out in a rush. He took the steps two at a time, his breath coming in shallow, quick bursts. The dusty cardboard box in the corner held his old elementary school notebooks. His hands shook slightly as he tore the tape away, tossing aside old math worksheets. He had to find it. He had to show her. A massive grin stretched across his face as his fingers brushed the spine of his old blue binder. The magic was real, and it was downstairs at the coffee table.

I spilled my tea when I saw the purple scales on Lily’s paper. "Who is that?" I asked, my voice pitching up a full octave. Lily chewed her lip and said, "That’s Gogo. He likes marshmallows." My heart did a wild little flip. I pulled my chair closer, my knees bumping the table, my eyes glued to the paper. "Does he? Does he also wear mismatched socks?" I pressed, leaning in so far my nose almost touched the crayon wax. Lily’s eyes went wide, and she nodded furiously. I let out a loud, sudden laugh, clapping my hands over my mouth. I couldn't sit still, my foot tapping a frantic rhythm against the linoleum. "Draw more," I urged her, sliding the whole box of crayons across the table with a sweep of my arm. "Draw everything he does. I want to see it all!"

The chalk squeaked against the pavement as Chloe drew a dog with butterfly wings. Marcus froze, the leash of his real dog slipping slightly in his grip. "Pip?" he breathed. He dropped to his knees right there on the dusty concrete, ignoring the dirt staining his good slacks. He snatched a piece of blue chalk from his niece's bucket. "Does he have a silver collar?" Marcus asked, his hand moving in quick, frantic strokes beside her drawing, adding the details he knew by heart. His chest buzzed with a sudden, electric warmth. He looked at Chloe, a massive, uncontainable smile breaking across his face. "Does he fly backwards when he sneezes?" Chloe gasped. "You know him?!" Marcus threw his head back and laughed, the sound echoing across the empty playground. "Know him? Pass me the green chalk, kiddo. Let me show you his treehouse."

I slammed the fridge door shut, making the bottles inside rattle violently. "Emma!" I shouted, my feet carrying me down the carpeted hallway before she even had a chance to answer. I was practically bouncing on my toes when I found her sitting in the den. I held her sketchbook paper out, my fingers trembling just enough to make the page rustle. "Where did you get this guy?" I asked, a breathless giggle slipping out of my chest. Emma looked up from her tablet. "That's Mr. Nimbus. He visits me at night." I dropped onto the beanbag beside her, my heart hammering a frantic, joyful rhythm against my ribs. My mind spun at a hundred miles an hour. "Tell me everything," I pleaded, grabbing her small hands. "Does he still sing the moon song? Oh, please tell me he still sings the moon song!"

Sarah scanned the corkboard at her niece's elementary school, politely admiring the crayon turkeys. Then, she saw it. Tucked in the corner was a sketch of a tall, spindly creature wearing a monocle made of daisies. Sir Flapjack. Sarah let out a sharp gasp, covering her mouth with both hands. She spun around, her eyes darting through the crowded classroom until she spotted seven-year-old Mia. Sarah practically shoved past two other parents, her boots clicking rapidly against the linoleum. She scooped Mia up under the arms, swinging her around in a dizzying circle. "Auntie Sarah!" Mia squeaked. Sarah set her down, kneeling so they were eye-level. "Mia, the daisy man on the board," Sarah spoke in a fast, hushed whisper, a massive grin splitting her face. "Did he ask you for extra syrup? We have to go to the store right now. Grab your coat!"

The thunder rattled the windowpanes, but I couldn't hear it over the rushing in my ears. I stared at the iPad screen in Sophie’s lap. She had used a digital brush to paint a bright orange yeti with roller skates. My old protector, Mango. I leaped off the sofa, knocking my throw pillow onto the floor. "Don't move a muscle, Soph!" I commanded, darting into the hallway. I dug frantically through the hall closet, throwing umbrellas and old coats over my shoulder until my fingers closed around the cold metal of my old roller skates. I rushed back into the living room, completely out of breath, my face flushed and hot. I dropped the skates onto the rug with a heavy thud. "If Mango is back," I said, a wide, unstoppable smile pulling at my cheeks, "then we need to clear the furniture. Right now!"

David stared at the watercolor painting drying on the easel. It was a perfect rendition of Captain Starfish, complete with the eye-patch and pirate hat. His chest tightened, a swarm of butterflies erupting in his stomach. He looked down at his niece, Penny, who was washing her brushes. "Penny," David said, his voice cracking slightly. He began pacing the small room, his hands running through his hair, unable to stand still. He stopped, picked up a toy sword, and pointed it at the ceiling. "Did the Captain say anything about the buried treasure under the oak tree?" Penny gasped, her eyes going round. "He said you hid it!" David threw his head back and let out a booming laugh. He tossed the toy sword onto the bed and grabbed his shoes. "Put your boots on, Penny! We’ve got a hole to dig!"

The pixels on my laptop screen stabilized, showing my niece holding up a piece of notebook paper. "This is Zog," she announced. I leaned in so close my nose bumped the screen. Zog.
